He further emphasizes that defendant 1 named Begum Rezia 
Khatun executed a registered kabala deed number 1921 in 
February 1996 in favour of Sheikh Abu Naser wherein she 
herself stated that she had obtained settlement of 19.15 acres 
of land from the District Collector, Khulna on 18.09.1946  in 
Miscellaneous Case 54 of 1946-47 but by virtue of orders 
dated 15.11.1954 passed in Miscellaneous Case 43 of 1953-54 
and dated 15.05.1969 passed by the Additional Deputy 
Commissioner (Revenue) in Miscellaneous Appeal 10 of 
1955-56 and by virtue of the order dated 25.05.1969 passed by 
the Secretary, Ministry of Land Reforms all such settlement 
deeds were cancelled and as such defendant 1 has no valid title 
or possession in the suit land and the Government had no 
authority to settle the same in her favour. Consequently the 
appellate Court rightly rejected the applications for addition of 
party filed by the present petitioners claiming through her. In 
support of his submission learned Adovate has referred to the 
cases of Md. Miksar Ali Dewan and others Vs. Dares Ali 

<<PAGE 20>>
 
20
Mondal and others, 13 MLR(AD) 105; Lakshan Chandra 
Mandal Vs. Takim Dhali and others, 28 CWN 1033; Ahmed 
Bepari and others Vs. Toki Mahomed and others, 8 CLJ 538; 
Bangladesh Vs. Md. Salam and others, 5 BCR(AD) 366; ADC 
Revenue Vs. Md. Riazuddin, 5 BLC(AD) 76; Sher 
Mohammad Vs. Sarada Bala Sen, 45 DLR 527; Adamjee Sons 
Ltd. Vs. Jiban Bima Corporation, 45 DLR 89; Chairman 
RAJUK and others Vs. A. Rouf Chowdhury and others, 8 
BLT(AD) 279 and finally submits that the rule having no 
merit may be discharged.  
The learned Deputy Attorney General Mr. Md. Yousuf 
Ali referring to Order 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure along 
with the Bangladesh Law Officers Order, 1972 (President’s 
Order Number 6 of 1972) and the Gazette Notification dated 
23.03.1973 issued by the Law Division of the Ministry of Law 
and Parliamentary Affairs submits that although he has not 
filed any formal power he is legally entitled to defend the 
interest of the Government.  
The learned Deputy Attorney General while generally 
concurring with the submissions advanced by the learned 
Advocate for the petitioners further submits that R.S. record 

<<PAGE 21>>
 
21
number 1 prepared in the name of defendant 122 
(Government) having not been rebutted by any cogent, reliable  
and admissible evidence carries a presumption of correctness 
under Section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 
Since the plaintiffs failed to establish their title and possession 
in the suit land the suit was rightly dismissed by the trial Court 
and he prays for making the Rule absolute.        
Heard the learned Advocates of both sides and perused 
the materials on record.  
In this revision Rule was issued on the following terms:  
“Let a Rule be issued calling upon the 
opposite parties 1-179 to show cause as to why the 
impugned Order 36 dated 16.06.2014 passed by the 
learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, 
Khulna in Title Appeal No. 11 of 2012 rejecting 
applications for addition of party and adjournment 
thereby allowing the appeal by judgment and 
decree dated 16.06.2014 after setting aside the 
judgment and decree dated 02.10.2011 passed by 
the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Khulna 
in Title Suit No. 687 of 1978 should not be set 

<<PAGE 22>>
 
22
aside and/or pass such other or further order or 
orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.” 
 
 It appears that petitioners 1-12 are subsequent 
transferees from defendant 1 who is now opposite party 
number 180 named Rezia Khatun and petitioner number 13 
namely Halim Beg is defendant number 74 in the suit. 
Admittedly petitioners 1-12 were not parties to the suit. The 
record further reveals that the instant Title Suit 687 of 1978 
was dismissed on 16.07.1994 in presence of defendants 1, 74, 
78, 122 and 131 and decree was drawn up on 23.07.1994. The 
plaintiffs thereafter preferred First Appeal 317 of 1994 before 
the High Court Division and upon hearing a Division Bench 
set aside the judgment and decree of the trial Court and 
remanded the suit by judgment and decree 07.03.2010. After 
remand the Trial Court received the record on 11.07.2010 and 
restored the suit to its original file and number and fixed on 
27.07.2010 for taking necessary steps with a direction to 
inform the learned Advocates of both sides. However from the 
certified copy of the order dated 11.07.2010 Annexure-D read 
with the order sheet it appears that the office of the Court 
informed only the Government pleader representing defendant 
number 122 while the learned Advocates representing the 

<<PAGE 23>>
 
23
other contesting defendants were not notified as a result of 
which they failed to contest the suit despite having filed 
written 
statements. 
Consequently 
the 
suit 
proceeded 
practically against defendant number 122 alone and was 
ultimately dismissed by judgment and decree dated 
02.10.2011. The plaintiffs then preferred Title Appeal 11 of 
2012 which was registered on 23.01.2012. On the same date 
the plaintiffs filed an application for dispensing with the 
service of notice upon defendant-respondents 2-131 which 
was allowed by Order Number 3 dated 26.01.2012. Thus it is 
evident that the defendants particularly those who had earlier 
contested the suit remained completely unaware of both the 
suit proceedings after remand and the appeal.  
 
It further appears that petitioners 1-12 upon coming to 
know of the appeal filed applications on 10.06.2014 and 
16.06.2014 for being added as parties in the appeal  relying 
upon inter alia the decision reported in 44 DLR 465 
(Padmabati case) as apparent from  Annexure-G series and H 
series. However the appellate Court without assigning any 
reason whatsoever rejected those applications and on the same 
day proceeded to allow the appeal by passing the impugned 
judgment and decree on 16.06.2014.  

<<PAGE 24>>
 
24
 
It is also found that defendant number 74 who is now 
petitioner number 13 filed an application on 11.06.2014 in the 
appeal stating that after remand he was kept in the dark and 
was not informed of the proceedings which is evident from 
Annexure “I” to the revisional application. The appellate 
Court however rejected the said application without assigning 
any cogent reason merely observing that the contention was 
not satisfactory. This Court is constrained to observe that such 
conduct of the appellate Court particulaly Order Number 36 
dated 16.06.2014 strikes at the very root of the principles of 
natural justice. The appellate Court failed to appreciate that 
when a suit is remanded it is incumbent upon the trial Court to 
issue fresh notice to the parties or their engaged Advocates 
and to ensure their participation in the proceedings. The 
failure to serve notice upon the contesting defendants after 
remand is a fatal irregularity vitiating the entire proceeding.  
In this regard the provisions of Order 3 Rule 4 of the Code of 
Civil Procedure read with Rules 63, 93, 388 of the Civil Rules 
and Orders and Rule 466(2) of the erstwhile High Court Civil 
Rules and Orders mandate proper communication with the 
learned Advocates. This principle has been affirmed in the 
cases of M.A. Wahab and another Vs. Abul Kalam and 

<<PAGE 25>>
 
25
another reported in 11 BLD(AD) 274 and Kashaituli Jame 
Mosque Wakf Estate Vs. Md. Abdus Salam Bepari and others 
reported in 1 LM(AD) 239=7 ALR(AD) 204. The omission to 
notify the learned Advocates of the contesting defendants is 
thus a gross violation of settled procedure and has resulted in 
serious miscarriage of justice. Moreover it is particularly 
noteworthy again that in the appeal by order 3 dated 
26.01.2012 service of notice upon this defendant was 
dispensed with upon prayer by the plaintiffs and the same was 
allowed. Accordingly this defendant had no prior knowledge 
of the appeal.  
 
As regards the objection raised by the opposite parties 
that petitioners 1-12 being third parties are not competent to 
maintain the present revisional application it appears that in 
the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case no effective 
alternative remedy has been shown to be available to them. 
Moreover petitioner number 13 is admittedly a party to the 
suit. Therefore this Rule is maintainable at least at his instance 
and in the facts of the case can also proceed at the instance of 
petitioners 1-12. This view finds support from the decisions in 
Ismail Hossain Vs. Shakhina and others, 17 BLC 320 and 

<<PAGE 26>>
 
26
Abdul Jalil and others Vs. Shah Alam and others, 16 BLC 
492.    
 
Turning now to the merits of the case it appears that the 
plaintiffs numbering as many as 148 claimed declaration of 
title over 680 acres of land. However the plaint does not 
clearly disclose from which landlord or under which specific 
plot numbers the alleged 129 acres of land were settled in the 
year 1338 B.S. The subsequent claims of settlement of further 
129 acres in 1348 B.S. and 203 acres in 1352 B.S. are also 
vague and uncertain lacking any specific particulars.      
 
The plaintiffs have thus failed to establish with clarity 
and certainty the source of their title. There is no reliable oral 
or documentary evidence to show that any identifiable 
landlord settled the land in their favour. The evidence adduced 
by the plaintiffs is vague, inconsistent and devoid of probative 
value.  
 
Although numerous documents were produced and 
marked as exhibits but none of them either individually or 
collectively is sufficient to prove the plaintiffs’ title to the suit 
land measuring 680 acres. The alleged amalnama (Exhibit-52) 
which is claimed to be the principal document of title has not 

<<PAGE 27>>
 
27
been proved in accordance with law. The claim that the 
original was lost is not substantiated by reliable evidence and 
the so called General Diary Exhibit-2 was not properly 
proved. Moreover it appears from the record that an amalnama 
as indicated by the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs is still 
available in the case file though blurred which casts serious 
doubt on the alleged loss of the original. Therefore the 
authenticity of Exhibit-52 becomes highly questionable.  
 
The appellate Court erred in treating Exhibit-52 as a 
certified copy whereas it does not bear the essential legal 
characteristics of a certified copy as required under sections 
75, 76, 77 and 79 of the Evidence Act. In absence of proper 
proof of the original document or a legally admissible certified 
copy Exhibit-52 is inadmissible in evidence and has no 
evidentiary value according to Sections 61, 63, 65, 67, 68, 75, 
76, 77 and 79 of the Evidence Act. A certified copy must 
contain a clear endorsement that it is true copy of the original 
and must also bear the signature and official seal of the 
authorised officer and the date of issuance. Under Section 57 
of the Registration Act only the Registrar or Sub-Registrar is 
legally empowered to grant certified copies of registered 
instruments. Similarly in the case of Court documents only the 

<<PAGE 28>>
 
28
Copying Department of the concerned Court under the 
supervision of authorised officer is competent to issue 
certified copies of records forming part of the judicial file. In 
the present case the alleged amalnama is admittedly an 
unregistered private document. Therefore Exhibit-52 itself is 
never a certified copy and the same is fabricated.   
 
Similarly Exhibit-8 being a deed of relinquishment 
cannot by itself confer title. It is at best a corroborative 
document and in absence of a valid primary source of title it 
cannot sustain the plaintiffs’ claim. Moreover Exhibit-8 never 
shows as to how the predecessor of defendant 1 became owner 
of the entire 680 acres of land as claimed by the plaintiffs. On 
the other hand the primary source of title Exhibit-52 has in no 
manner been proved in evidence. Furthermore the evidence of 
P.W. 2 who purportedly witnessed Exhibit-8 is inherently 
unreliable as his age indicates that he could not have 
witnessed a document executed in 1962. This renders the 
document highly suspicious.  
 
It also appears that no rent receipts were ever filed 
although the appellate Court placed reliance upon them out of 
thin air. Exhibit-4 being merely an order of a revenue officer 

<<PAGE 29>>
 
29
does not establish title over the entire suit land. Exhibit-4 does 
not mention or include the entire 680 acres of suit property. 
From paragraph 6 of the plaint it transpires that as many as 63 
kabalas executed from the year 1967 to 1975 have been 
alleged to have been relied upon by the defendants but 
plaintiffs did not seek any relief in respect of those documents. 
Since the said documents have remained outstanding and 
subsisting and continue to operate as a legal bar against the 
plaintiffs’ claim of title the instant suit is clearly barred under 
Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.  
 
The plaintiffs have also failed to implead necessary 
parties including recorded tenants and the Mutawalli of the 
Waqf property thereby rendering the suit defective for non-
joinder of necessary parties.  
 
Upon consideration of the submissions of the learned 
Advocates for the respective parties and on perusal of the 
evidence on record it appears that Exhibit-52 being devoid of 
any legal basis and evidentiary value fails to challenge or 
weaken the presumption attached to Exhibit-Ka. Although the 
plaintiffs have claimed that they obtained settlement of the suit 
land since 1338 B.S. it is evident that in none of the 

<<PAGE 30>>
 
30
subsequent surveys was the suit land recorded in their names. 
No rent receipt in respect of the suit land in the names of the 
plaintiffs has been produced or proved before the Court. 
Therefore it transpires that there is no documentary evidence 
whatsoever in support of the alleged possession of the 
plaintiffs over the suit property.  
 
P.W. 2 in his deposition claimed that the plaintiffs had 
been possessing the suit land for the last 50-60 years but in 
cross-examination he admitted that he did not know the total 
number of plaintiffs nor did he know all of them personally 
and he could not specify who was in possession of which 
portion of the land nor even the total area of the suit land. 
Similarly P.W. 3 in his cross-examination admitted that out of 
148 plaintiffs he was unable to state who was in possession of 
what extent of land. Such admission seriously undermines the 
claim of possession made by the plaintiffs. P.W. 4 in his cross-
examination stated that he was merely a Mohorar and his work 
was limited to pulling the chain rope and he could not produce 
any document to show that he had worked under Ashraf or 
Ahad. His evidence therefore does not support the case of the 
plaintiffs in any material particular.  

<<PAGE 31>>
 
31
 
The appellate Court however while deciding the question 
of possession observed that P.W. 1 had given detailed 
supporting evidence and P.W. 2 Jamal Ghazi along with P.W. 
3 Bilal Mazi and P.W. 4 Manohar Chandra Roy had all 
supported the claim of the plaintiffs’ possession over the suit 
land. But upon careful scrutiny of their depositions it is found 
that their statements are inconsistent, uncertain and fail to 
establish actual, continuous and specific possession of the 
plaintiffs over any definite portion of the suit property.  
 
It is an undisputed fact on record that despite the 
plaintiffs’ assertion of holding the land since 1338 B.S. the 
suit land was never recorded in their names in any subsequent 
official survey. No record-of-right or survey entry has been 
produced to show that either title or possession of the land was 
ever reflected in their favour. The findings on possession 
arrived at by the trial Court were not properly confronted or 
reversed by the appellate Court in accordance with the 
provisions of Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil 
Procedure. The appellate Court failed to advert to and 
reappraise the trial Court’s crucial findings regarding the 
credibility 
and 
cogency 
of 
the 
evidence. 
Upon 
a 
comprehensive evaluation of the entire evidence on record it 

<<PAGE 32>>
 
32
appears that plaintiffs have failed to produce any reliable 
documentary or convincing oral evidence identifying specific 
possession establishing a chain of settlement or proving 
continuous, uninterrupted and exclusive possession so as to 
sustain a valid claim of title.  
 
Furthermore P.W. 1 in his cross-examination admitted 
that the entire suit land is situated in one compact block. P.W. 
3 also admitted that the suit land lies in one single compact 
area. However the schedule to the plaint clearly describes the 
suit land as comprising three separate and distinct boundaries. 
This material inconsistency between the oral evidence and the 
description in the plaint renders the identity of the suit land 
uncertain and vague. Consequently the suit is liable to be 
dismissed for want of proper specification and identification 
of the suit land.   
 
The contention of the plaintiffs that their possession 
stands proved by the report of the Advocate Commissioner 
and by the order passed by this Court in matter of temporary 
injunction is also devoid of merit. It is a settled proposition of 
law that an Advocate Commissioner has no authority to 
determine possession of any party. Such determination must 

<<PAGE 33>>
 
33
be made by the Court itself upon proper appreciation of the 
evidence on record. It is also a settled principle that any 
observation made in an interlocutory or incidental proceeding 
does not have any binding effect at the time of final 
adjudication of the suit on merits.  
 
In view of the foregoing discussions it appears that the 
appellate Court committed error of law resulting in an error in 
such decree occasioning failure of justice in decreeing the suit 
upon fanciful consideration. Accordingly the judgment and 
decree passed by the Court of appeal below cannot be 
sustained in law.  
 
In the result the Rule is made absolute. 
 
The order of stay passed by this Court stands vacated.  
Let a copy of this judgment be communicated to the 
Court concerned forthwith and the Lower Court Records be 
sent down immediately.  
 
 
Md. Ali Reza, J: 
 
 
 
  
 
 
 
Naher-B.O
input_summary: In December 1978, plaintiff OPPOSITE PARTIES sued for title over 680 acres of accreted riverine char land, claiming landlord settlements from 1338 to 1356 B.S. via amalnama at Tk. 9.50 rent and forty years' possession. First defendant pleaded her husband PERSON_1's 1962 decree under the Bengal Alluvial Lands Act, 1920 over 32.78 acres, while the Government pleaded vesting under Sections 86 and 87 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. After a 2010 High Court remand, only Government counsel received notice; the suit failed in October 2011, and plaintiffs obtained appellate notice dispensation in January 2012. On 16.06.2014, the appellate court turned down party-addition pleas by 2009-2011 purchasers PETITIONERS 1 to 12 and defendant PETITIONER 13's adjournment plea and decreed the appeal. PETITIONERS and Government counsel alleged unnotified remand, unproved amalnama, and Section 42 Specific Relief Act bars.
explanation: UNCERTAIN: Alongside Order 3 Rule 4 and Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, the Court substantially applied Sections 61, 63, 65, 67, 68, 75-77, and 79 of the Evidence Act 1872 and Section 42 of the Specific Relief Act. Omitting post-remand notice to contesting defendants' counsel, dispensing with appellate notice, and turning down party-addition and adjournment pleas without reasons violated natural justice and Order 3 Rule 4. On merits, the unregistered private amalnama lacked valid secondary proof, 63 unchallenged deeds (1967-1975) and omitted parties barred declaratory relief, and reversing possession findings without reappraisal breached Order 41 Rule 31.

Bench:

Shoili Abashan Ltd and another

In the instant revision Rule was issued calling upon the 
opposite party 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and 
order dated 17.02.2025 passed by the learned District Judge, 
Dhaka in Miscellaneous Appeal Number 35 of 2025 
disallowing the appeal thereby affirming the judgment and 
order dated 09.03.2023 passed by the learned Joint District 
Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka in Title Suit Number 17 of 2023 
allowing the application for temporary injunction should not 
be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders be 
passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.  

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
Opposite party as plaintiff filed Title Suit 17 of 2023 on 
10.01.2023 in the Court of Joint District Judge, 4th Court, 
Dhaka for specific performance of contract on the contention 
that plaintiff entered into an agreement on 20.01.2021 with the 
defendant who received taka 15 lac on 20.01.2021 as earnest 
money out of total consideration of taka 70 (seventy) lac. 
Subsequently defendant after receiving the entire money did 
not register the kabala. Finally when defendant was served 
with notices on 3 occasions but did not take step to register the 
kabala plaintiff filed the instant suit.  
In the suit plaintiff filed an application for temporary 
injunction under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 read with Section 151 
of the Code of Civil Procedure on 18.01.2023 on the 
contention that defendant 1 has been threatening the plaintiff 
with transfer the suit flat elsewhere in view to harass the 
plaintiff and for illegal gain. Plaintiff-applicant has good 
prima facie case and the balance of convenience and 
inconvenience is in his favour and in favour of granting 
injunction prayed for and he will suffer irreparable loss and 
injury in the event of any illegal transfer made to the detriment 
of his interest.  

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
Notice was issued upon the defendant to show cause 
within 7 days which after return was kept with the record. 
Subsequently on 01.03.2023 plaintiff filed another application 
for ad interim injunction under Section 151 of the Code of 
Civil Procedure till hearing of the original application. Trial 
Court heard the application and allowed the same by judgment 
and order dated 09.03.2023 on the finding that plaintiff has got 
prima facie arguable case and defendant is restrained from 
transferring the suit flat till disposal of the suit.   
As against the same defendant preferred Miscellaneous 
Appeal 35 of 2025 before the District Judge, Dhaka on 
10.02.2025 which was out of time of 668 days and for such 
reason an application for condonation of delay was also filed.  
Appellate Court dismissed the appeal summarily on 
17.02.2025 being barred by law of limitation on the finding 
that such a long delay of 668 days constitutes gross negligence 
and such delay was not explained to satisfaction.  
As against the order dated 17.02.2025 passed by the 
appellate Court defendant as petitioner preferred this revision 
and obtained Rule on 19.03.2025.  
Learned Advocate Ms. Salma Sultana appearing on 
behalf of the petitioners submits that the appellate Court upon 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
misinterpretation of law and fact of the case and without going 
into the merit of the case wrongfully rejected the appeal 
summarily on ground of delay which cannot be sustained in 
the eye of law and the appellate Court thus committeed error 
of law resulting in an error in such order occasioning failure of 
justice. She then submits that the appellate Court failed to 
appreciate that defendant is the exclusive owner in possession 
of the suit property and the plaintiff has got no prima facie 
arguable case thus the impugned order is bad in law and the 
appellate Court committed error of law occasioning failure of 
justice in dismissing the appeal summarily. She further 
submits that the appellate Court did not consider that the 
balance of convenience and inconvenience is in favour of 
defendant and the order of injunction passed by the trial Court 
is operating harshly against the defendant and the judgment 
and order passed by the appellate Court being perverse and 
misconceived is liable to be interfered with by this Court in 
revision. She points out that the appellate Court committed 
wrong in not considering the merit of the case and dismissal of 
the appeal only considering the ground of condonation of 
delay was not proper for which justice came undone and the 
defendant suffers irreparable loss and injury and the impugned 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
judgment being passed not in accordance with law is liable to 
be 
set 
aside. 
She 
introduced 
some 
documents 
in 
supplementary affidavit dated 16.03.2025 but did not adduce 
the application for condonation of delay filed in appeal. She 
refers to the case of Haji Md. Elias and another Vs. Mrs. 
Suraya Rahman reported in 1 BLD(AD) 147 and finally 
submits that in view of the ratio laid down in the referred case 
this injunction cannot be granted.  
Learned Advocate Mr. Subrata Saha appearing on behalf 
of the opposite party submits that since defendant admitted 
part payment of the total consideration plaintiff has got good 
arguable prima facie case and the balance of convenience and 
inconvenience is in favour of the plaintiff and in the event of 
any transfer the opposite party shall suffer irreparable loss and 
injury because such transfer inevitably invites multiplicity of 
proceedings with untold misery and harassment. He contends 
that 
injunction 
was 
passed 
on 
09.03.2023 
and 
a 
comprehensive time was consumed in filing the appeal and the 
appellate Court correctly rejected the appeal on ground of 
limitation in that the application for condonation of delay 
nowhere shows any reasonable ground or explanation to 
satisfy the minimum legal requirement. He also submits that 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
the fact and circumstance of 1 BLD case do not attract the fact 
of the present case. He points out that the impugned order 
being related to condonation of delay is other than the fact of 
granting temporary injunction and if the explanation offered to 
the application for condonation of delay is not satisfactory the 
petitioner has no case and the Rule is liable to be discharged.  
Heard the learned Advocates for both sides and perused 
the materials on record and also gone through the impugned 
judgments passed by the Courts below. 
It appears that the application for condonation of delay 
in filing the appeal under Section 5 of the Limitation Act is 
neither filed in the revisional application nor with the 
supplementary affidavit dated 09.12.2025. During the course 
of hearing of revision when the application for condonation of 
delay filed in appeal under section 5 of the Limitation Act was 
called for the learned counsel representing the petitioner 
produced an office copy of the same before the Court. Upon 
careful examination of the same it transpires that the 
application comprises 4 paragraphs but none of those 
paragraphs contains any satisfactory and plausible or legally 
tenable explanation for the inordinate delay of 668 days. The 
application merely asserts that the delay was not deliberate on 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
the part of the petitioner and due to the petitioner’s lack of 
communication with his councel in appeal coupled with the 
misleading assurances of payment allegedly given by the 
opposite party as well as the petitioner’s limited understanding 
the appeal could not be filed in time.  
An application devoid of any cogent and substantive or 
acceptable explanation for such an extraordinary lapse of time 
cannot be entertained in the eye of law. Furtheremore the 
effort made by the petitioner to set up a third case by annexing 
various documents through a supplementary affidavit is also 
devoid of legal merit and cannot be accepted.  
The trial Court granted temporary injunction on 
09.03.2023. Thereafter the appeal was filed on 10.02.2025 
after almost 2 years of the order of injunction. During this 
substantial interval of nearly 2 years it appears that the 
petitioner had no grievance against the order otherwise such 
an inordinate delay in preferring the appeal would not have 
occurred.  
At the present stage unless and until the delay is 
condoned the petitioner is not entitled to a hearing on the merit 
of the injunction matter. The question of examining the prima 
facie case and balance of convenience or irreparable loss does 

<<PAGE 8>>
 
8
not arise in favour of the petitioner until the delay stands 
lawfully waived.  
Since no reasonable or legally sustainable grounds exist 
for condoning such a prolonged delay under Section 5 of the 
Limitation Act it is evident that the appellate Court rendered 
the judgment both judiciously and in conformity with law. 
Consequently the judgment of the appellate Court being 
correct and well-reasoned does not warrant any interference.  
Therefore I find no merit in this Rule.  
In the result the Rule is discharged.  
However the trial Court is directed to dispose of the suit 
as expeditiously as possible preferably within 6(six) months 
from the receipt of this judgment.  
The order of stay passed by this Court stands vacated.  
Communicate this judgment to the concerned Court at 
once.  
 
 
Md. Ali Reza, J:

input_summary: In January 2023, OPPOSITE PARTY sued PETITIONERS for specific performance of a 20.01.2021 flat-purchase agreement priced at Tk. 70 lac, alleging PETITIONERS took Tk. 15 lac earnest money and later received the full balance yet ignored three notices to register the sale deed. Applying under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 and Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure to prevent alienation of the flat, OPPOSITE PARTY secured a temporary injunction on 09.03.2023 restraining transfer until suit disposal. Filing a miscellaneous appeal 668 days late on 10.02.2025 with a condonation petition, PETITIONERS faced summary termination of the appeal as time-barred on 17.02.2025. Seeking revision, PETITIONERS argued the appellate court ignored their exclusive possession, balance of convenience, and supplementary documents, whereas OPPOSITE PARTY cited admitted part-payment and the unexplained 668-day delay.
explanation: Inspecting the office copy of PETITIONERS' four-paragraph condonation petition under Section 5 of the Limitation Act 1908—omitted from both the revisional petition and supplementary affidavits—the Court found only vague assertions of poor counsel communication, alleged payment assurances, and limited understanding, furnishing no tenable ground for a nearly two-year, 668-day delay after the 09.03.2023 injunction. Holding that an appellant cannot be heard on temporary-injunction merits or introduce new supplementary-affidavit defences unless delay is first lawfully condoned under Section 5, the Court declined revisional interference and directed suit disposal preferably within six months.

In the instant revision Rule was issued on 14.07.2025 
calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the 
order dated 03.06.2025 passed by the learned District Judge, 
Chattogram in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 179 of 2025 not 
passing an ad interim order of temporary injunction as per 
prayer of an application for temporary injunction filed by the 
plaintiff-appellant-petitioner should not be set aside and/or 
such other of further order or orders passed as to this Court

The petitioner in the instant Civil Revision preferred 
Other Suit Number 30 of 2021 on 21.01.2021 seeking 
declaration that deed number 4578 dated 11.06.2020 is false, 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
forged, fraudulent, illegal, without jurisdiction, collusive, 
manufactured, inoperative and a mere paper transaction and 
not binding upon the plaintiff. A further declaration was 
sought that record of right (R.O.R) number 1665 prepared in 
the names of defendants 3-5 is erroneous, collusive, incorrect 
and not binding upon the plaintiff.  
After lapse of approximately four years from the 
institution of the suit the plaintiff filed an application for 
temporary injunction on 20.11.2024 under order 39 rules 1 and 
2 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying 
for an order of temporary injunction against defendants 1 and 
2. Defendants 1 and 2 entered appearance and filed written 
statement and objection to the application for injunction on 
26.01.2025.  
The substance of the plaint and the application for 
injunction is that on the strength of the deed number 4578 
dated 11.06.2020 allegedly executed by defendants 3-5 in 
favour of defendants 1 and 2 the latter mutated their names 
and are attempting to dispossess the plaintiff illegally from the 
suit land and to forcibly trespass thereupon to disturb the 
plaintiff’s peaceful possession and to transfer the same to third 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
parties thereby causing irreparable loss and injury to the 
plaintiff.  
On the contrary the contesting defendants categorically 
denied the allegations and contended that they purchased 12 
decimals of the suit land on 11.06.2020 from the B.S. recorded 
owners and opened a holding and disclosed the property 
before the income tax authority and obtained electricity 
connection and have been possessing the land by constructing 
permanent boundary wall on all sides. According to them the 
statements made in the injunction petition are false and 
misconceived.  
From the pleadings and materials on record it appears 
that the previous owner of the plaintiff namely Ruhul amin 
and the previous owner of the defendants namely Abdur 
Rashid purchased land from the same recorded owner Ambiya 
on the same date on 23.10.1984. The deed in favour of Abdur 
Rashid bears number 18413 whereas the deed in favour of 
Ruhul amin bears number 18414. The deed bearing number 
18413 therefore prima facie appears to have been executed 
earlier in point of time.  
The trial Court after hearing both sides and upon framing 
four issues rejected the application for temporary injunction 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
by order dated 09.04.2025 upon discussion of the pleadings 
and materials on record. The trial Court observed that the 
schedule and specification of the suit land as described in the 
plaintiff’s deed are vague and indistinct whereas from the 
defendants’ deed and khatian a prima facie case in their favour 
is discernible.  
Being aggrieved the plaintiff preferred Miscellaneous 
Appeal Number 179 of 2025 under Order XLIII Rule 1(r) of 
the Code of Civil Procedure with a delay of 56 days. From the 
impugned order number 1 dated 03.06.2025 it transpires that 
although the appellate Court did not formally allow the 
application under Section 5 of the Limitation Act it 
provisionally accepted the appeal for hearing and issued a 
show cause notice upon defendants 1 and 2 for 15 days as to 
why an order of temporary injunction should not be granted. 
Challenging the said order the present revision has been filed 
and this Court by order dated 14.07.2025 issued Rule along 
with an ad interim order of status quo.  
Mr. Mohammad Rezaul Hossain (Morshed), learned 
Advocate for the petitioner submits that the Court of appeal 
below committed an error of law resulting in failure of justice 
by passing the impugned order without considering the settled 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
principles governing grant of temporary injunction namely 
existence of a prima facie case and balance of convenience 
and likelihood of irreparable loss. He further submits that the 
impugned order is a non-speaking order passed upon 
misconception of law and is therefore liable to be set aside in 
exercise of revisional jurisdiction under Section 115(1) of the 
Code of Civil Procedure. He lastly prays that the Rule having 
merit be made absolute.  
Conversely Mr. Muhammad Nawab Ali, learned 
Advocate for the opposite parties opposes the Rule and 
submits that there was no lawful justification for issuance of 
the Rule against a mere show cause notice and the revision is 
devoid of merit and liable to be discharged.  
Heard the learned Advocates of both sides and perused 
the lower Court records.  
It appears from the record that the trial Court after 
detailed hearing rejected the prayer for temporary injunction 
upon consideration of the relevant legal ingredients as 
required under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 of the Code of Civil 
Procedure. The appellate Court in exercise of its jurisdiction 
merely issued notice upon the respondents to show cause as to 
why injunction should not be granted and from the order sheet 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
it transpires that upon issuance of notice the defendants have 
already entered appearance.  
In such circumstances filing of the present revision 
before this Court without allowing the appellate Court to 
dispose of the injunction matter on merit does not appear to 
serve any legally acceptable purpose. The petitioner does not 
appear to have approached this Court with clean hands.  
It is further noteworthy that in paragraphs 9(a) and (b) of 
the plaint wherein the impugned deed and khatian have been 
challenged no description of the said deed or khatian has been 
incorporated in schedule 1 or schedule 1(a) of the plaint. It is 
not discernible from the schedule of the plaint whether the 
land covered by the impugned deed against which relief has 
been sought in the prayer portion of the plaint has at all been 
incorporated therein and it is further apparent that the 
impugned deed has not been referred to in the schedule to the 
plaint. Moreover from a plain reading of the plaint it appears 
that the plaintiff is not a party to the deed dated 11.06.2020 yet 
no specific prayer for declaration of his own title has been 
sought in clear terms. It is well settled that when a third party 
challenges a deed or decree he must first establish and seek 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
declaration of his own right, title and interest. In the instant 
suit no such comprehensive prayer is discernible. 
Additionally if the prayer for injunction had been of such 
pressing and paramount importance to the plaintiff he would 
not have allowed a delay of nearly 02(two) months in 
preferring the Miscellaneous appeal. Such delay reasonably 
leads to the inference that the order of injunction is being 
sought not out of genuine urgency but rather for achieving 
some collateral or ulterior purpose.  
In view of the discussions made hereinabove I find no 
substance in the Rule.  
Accordingly the Rule is discharged.  
The order of status quo passed by this Court stands 
vacated.  
Communicate this judgment to the concerned Court at 
once. 
The appellate Court is directed to dispose of the 
application 
for 
temporary 
injunction 
expeditiously in 
accordance with law without being influenced by any 
observation made herein which are confined solely for the 
purpose of disposal of this Rule.   
 
 
Md. Ali Reza, J: 
Naher-B.O
input_summary: In January 2021, PETITIONER sued to declare a 11.06.2020 sale deed (executed by defendants 3 to 5 for defendants 1 and 2) and defendants 3 to 5's record of rights forged and non-binding, seeking a temporary injunction nearly four years later in November 2024 under Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 read with Section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Defendants 1 and 2 pleaded buying 12 decimals from BS recorded owners and building a boundary wall, while October 1984 deeds from common owner PERSON_1 showed defendants' predecessor PERSON_2 held an earlier-numbered deed than PETITIONER's predecessor PERSON_3. After the trial court declined an injunction in April 2025, PETITIONER appealed 56 days late under Order XLIII Rule 1(r); on 03.06.2025 the appellate court issued only a 15-day show-cause notice, prompting revision against OPPOSITE PARTIES.
explanation: Reviewing the Order 39 Rules 1 and 2 record under the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, the Court held that where the trial court declined temporary injunction on merits and the appellate court merely issued a show-cause notice to which defendants had already appeared, bypassing appellate adjudication served no lawful purpose. Furthermore, the plaint schedules omitted any description of the challenged 11.06.2020 deed or khatian, PETITIONER as a non-party failed to seek a declaration of his own title, and a nearly two-month appellate delay negated genuine urgency, leaving the appellate court to decide the injunction plea expeditiously.

Bench:

Managing Director

In the instant revision Rule was issued on 22.05.2025 
calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the 
judgment and order dated 20.03.2025 passed by the District 
Judge, Dhaka in Execution Case No. 15 of 2024 allowing the 
application for attachment of immovable property under Order 
21 Rule 54 of the Code of Civil Procedure attaching the 
property mentioned in the schedule to the application should 
not be set aside and/or such other of further order or orders 
passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
The present opposite parties as petitioners filed a decree 
Execution Case 15 of 2024 before the District Judge, Dhaka 
for execution of consent award dated 02.03.2022 passed by the 
Arbitral Tribunal, Dhaka.  
The opposite parties being owners of 50 decimals of land 
of Central Road appertaining to Police Station Dhanmondi of 
District Dhaka entered into a deed of agreement on 18.10.2004 
with the present petitioner who is the developer for 
construction of a 15 storied commercial-cum-residential 
building. Subsequently upon arising of certain disputes the 
landowners namely the opposite parties sought arbitration and 
filed Arbitration Miscellaneous Case 756 of 2016 for 
constitution of arbitral tribunal and ultimately the tribunal was 
constituted with 3 members namely Mr. Justice Syed Amirul 
Islam as Chairman and Mr. Justice Nozrul Islam Chowdhury 
and Mr. Md. Shofiul Alam Mahmood as arbitrators. While the 
arbitration was going on the land owners and the developer 
agreed to settle their dispute amicably and signed a 
compromise agreement dated 18.10.2004 and upon their joint 
submission the learned arbitral tribunal passed an award on 
compromise on 02.03.2022.  

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
Since the developer namely the present petitioner failed 
to complete the project within the period stipulated in the 
compromise agreement the landowners filed Execution Case 
Number 15 of 2024 for realization of rent accrued to them in 
terms of the award.  
In the said execution case the landowners filed an 
application under Order 21 Rule 54 of the Code of Civil 
Procedure for attachment of the portion of the developer 
which was allowed by the District Judge by the impugned 
order 5 dated 20.03.2025.  
Challenging the said order the developer as petitioner 
filed the instant revision and obtained Rule on 22.05.2025. At 
the time of issuance of the Rule this Court was further pleased 
to stay the operation of the judgment and order dated 
20.03.2025 for a period of 01(one) year from date subject to 
the condition that the petitioner shall pay the total arrear of 
rent to the opposite parties within that period and also hand 
over the remaining incomplete flats to them and one third of 
the arrear rent is to be paid within 30 days and in that respect 
the Court directed the petitioner to submit an affidavit-of-
compliance showing payment of one third of the arrear rent as 
stated above.  

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
The opposite parties appeared in the Rule on 19.06.2025 
and filed an application bearing affidavit serial number 9543 
dated 07.07.2025 for vacating the order of stay for non-
compliance of the Court’s order dated 22.05.2025 contending 
that the petitioner in violation of the order of the Court by 
affidavit dated 07.07.2025 bearing affidavit Serial Number 
6843 showed payment by pay order of Tk. 14,08,800/- 
(fourteen lac eight thousand eight hundred) which amount is 
wholly inadequate and is contrary to the compromise award 
and the rule issuing order of this Court.   
It is further contended that as per the order of the Court 
the developer had to pay one third of the arrear rent which was 
for commercial portion of 40830 square feet at the rate of taka 
80 per month and for the residential 32 flats taka 30 thousand 
for each flat since April 2024 as contemplated in the award 
and thus the rent due for the commercial portion from April 
2024 to April 2025 is 40830 square feet at taka 80 per square 
feet per month for 12 months amounting to taka 3,91,96,800/- 
(three crore ninety one lac ninety six thousand eight hundred) 
and for the residential portion for 32 flats at taka 30 thousand 
per flat per month for 12 months amounting to taka 
1,15,20,000/- (one crore fifteen lac twenty thousand) totalling 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
taka 5,07,16,800/- (five crore seven lac sixteen thousand eight 
hundred). Therefore as per order of this Court one third of the 
total rent due up to April 2025 amounts to taka 5,07,16,800/- 
(five crore seven lac sixteen thousand eight hundred) which 
after divided by 3 equal to taka 1,69,05,600/- (one crore sixty 
nine lakh five thousand six hundred) which the petitioner was 
liable to pay to the opposite parties within 30 days from the 
date of the order. The developer however offered only taka 
14,08,800/- (fourteen lac eight thousand eight hundred) in 
place of 1,69,05,600/- (one crore sixty nine lac five thousand 
six hundred) which constitutes complete non-compliance with 
the order of this Court.  
Learned Advocate Mr. Purnindu Bikash Das along with 
Mr. Homayun Kabir Ahsan appearing on behalf of the 
petitioner submits that the Senior District Judge committed 
error of law resulting in an error in such order occasioning 
failure of justice in passing the impugned order which is 
apparently a non-speaking order being made without assigning 
any reason. He further submits that the opposite parties at their 
sweet will relied upon a vague schedule contrary to the 
consent award and compromise agreement to determine the 
amount allegedly due to them and the executing Court 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
disregarding the matter passed the impugned judgment in a 
slipshod manner thus committed error of law occasioning 
failure of justice. He points out that from reading of the 
application for execution it appears that the opposite parties 
claimed a total amount of taka 42,26,400/- (forty two lac 
twenty six thousand four hundred) as house rent but the 
executing Court directed to attach 32 residential flats and 
40830 square feet of commercial space which is manifestly 
excessive and disproportionate to the claim thus the impugned 
judgment is improper and misconceived. He further submits 
that the opposite parties obtained the order of attachment by 
suppressing crucial material facts that 7 flats have already 
been handed over to them and 17 flats are ready for delivery 
but the executing Court without adverting to this aspect of the 
case wrongly passed the order which has been operating 
harshly against the petitioner. He also contends that since the 
award was passed upon compromise agreement no party 
assumes the status of decree-holder or judgment-debtor and as 
such the application under Order 21 Rule 54 of the Code of 
Civil Procedure is misconceived but the executing Court failed 
to appreciate this material aspect thus committed error of law 
occasioning failure of justice. He lastly submits that since the 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
application for attachment was disposed of without notice the 
impugned order cannot be sustained for realization of movable 
property by attaching immovable property.  
On the other hand learned Advocate Mr. Taposh Kumar 
Dutta along with Ms. Ferdousi Akter appearing on behalf of 
the opposite parties takes me through the relevant paper of the 
record and refers to clause 1(c), 3 and 4 of the compromise 
agreement dated 23.09.2021 and submits that the execution 
was correctly filed in accordance with the award dated 
02.03.2022 taking its effect from the date of compromise 
agreement dated 23.09.2021 and the application for 
attachment under Order 21 Rule 54 in respect of schedule-Kha 
property has been lawfully filed as the matter originated in 
2004 and has remained unsolved to date notwithstanding that 
for this purpose both parties had agreed upon the compromise 
agreement wherein the opposite parties are legally entitled to 
seek their remedy under clause 3 and accordingly the 
executing court has rightly passed the judgment which in the 
present circumstances is not legally amenable to interference. 
He also submits that even if the impugned order is treated as a 
non-speaking order no legal irregularity arises therefrom 
because in the event of any illegal transfer of the property 

<<PAGE 8>>
 
8
under schedule-Kha the execution case would be frustrated 
and there being no error in passing the impugned order in 
furtherance of the execution proceeding the same is liable to 
be discharged.  
Heard the learned Advocates for both sides and perused 
the materials on record and also gone through the impugned 
order passed by the courts below. 
The opposite parties are the owners of the disputed 
property and the petitioners are the developers. For the 
purpose of construction of a 15 storied commercial-cum-
residential building an agreement was executed between the 
parties on 18.10.2004. Subsequently dispute arose between the 
parties and the opposite parties instituted Arbitration 
Miscellaneous Case Number 756 of 2016. In the said 
proceeding a 3 member arbitral tribunal was constituted 
comprising Mr. Justice Syed Amirul Islam as President and 
Mr. Justice Nozrul Islam Chowdhury and Mr. Md. Shafiqul 
Alam Mohammad as arbitrators in accordance with the 
Arbitration Act, 2001.  
During pendency of the arbitration proceedings the 
opposite parties and the developer agreed to amicably settle 
their disputes. In furtherance thereof a compromise agreement 

<<PAGE 9>>
 
9
was executed on 23.09.2021 which formed part of the original 
agreement dated 18.10.2004. On the basis of said compromise 
the arbitral tribunal passed an award on 02.03.2022 which is 
enforceable as a decree of the Court under Section 44 of the 
Arbitration Act 2001. 
It is evident from the record that the petitioner failed to 
implement the terms and conditions of the compromise 
agreement within the stipulated time particularly the 
obligations under clause 1, 3 and 4 thereof. Failure to comply 
with the terms of an award renders the award holder entitled to 
seek execution in the manner provided under law which is 
settled by illustration that an arbitral award stands on the same 
footing as a civil decree.  
Accordingly the opposite parties filed Execution Case 
Number 15 of 2024 on 26.11.2024 for realization of their 
accrued rent in terms of the award invoking Order 21 Rule 54 
of the Code of Civil Procedure. Notices were duly issued upon 
the judgment debtors in accordance with law. 
In the said execution case the opposite parties filed an 
application before the executing Court seeking attachment of 
the petitioner’s share described in the Kha schedule under 
Order 21 Rule 54 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Attachment 

<<PAGE 10>>
 
10
of immovable property under the said provision is a 
recognized mode of execution to prevent frustration of a 
decree by alienation.  
After service of notice and upon return thereof the 
petitioner failed to take any effective step or to discharge their 
decretal liability. The executing Court by order dated 
20.03.2025 allowed the application for attachment and passed 
the impugned judgment.  
Upon perusal of the record it appears that up to April 
2025 an amount of taka 5,07,16,800/- (five crore seven lac 
sixteen thousand eight hundred) fell due and outstanding on 
account of rent for the commercial and residential portions. 
From the rule issuing order it is evident that the petitioner was 
directed to deposit one third of the outstanding amount within 
30 days by filing an affidavit-of-compliance before this Court. 
One third of the aforesaid amount comes to taka 1,69,05,600/- 
(one crore sixty nine lac five thousand six hundred). However 
from 
the 
affidavit-in-compliance 
dated 
07.07.2025 
it 
transpires that the petitioner deposited only taka 14,08,800/- 
(fourteen lac eight thousand eight hundred) by pay order 
before the Court. Such payment manifestly falls far short of 

<<PAGE 11>>
 
11
the amount directed by the Court and clearly demonstrates that 
the petitioner has willfully ignored the order of the Court.  
The conduct of the petitioner further reveals an attempt 
to deprive the opposite parties of their lawful dues by adopting 
various means and methods which is wholly inconsistent with 
the principles of fairness and justice. Such conduct strikes at 
the very root of due administration of justice. In view of the 
above the affidavit-of-compliance filed by the petitioner 
cannot be held to be legally acceptable and does not amount to 
compliance with the order of this Court.  
The petitioner has raised the contention that since no 
specific amount was mentioned in the execution application 
attachment of the entire property is not lawful. This contention 
is misconceived. The compromise agreement itself contains 
clear stipulation with regard to the outstanding liabilities and 
mode of realization thereof. A plain reading of Order 41 Rule 
54 of the Code of Civil Procedure makes it abundantly clear 
that the said provision does not require prior determination or 
specification of the monetary value of the property sought to 
be attached. Attachment under the said provision is intended 
to restrain alienation of the property and does not amount to 
dispossession.   

<<PAGE 12>>
 
12
Attachment is thus a preventive measure to secure the 
ends of justice and to ensure that the execution proceedings 
are not rendered nugatory by transfer or encumbrance of the 
property.  
Immediately prior to the delivery of judgment the 
learned Advocate for the petitioner filed a supplementary-
affidavit and referred therein to Annexure-E which is a 
memorandum dated 25.11.2025 signed by the President of 
REHAB and addressed to all the members of REHAB. From 
the said memorandum it appears that REHAB communicated 
its own decision to its members. Relying upon the said letter 
the learned Advocate submitted that the present execution case 
is premature on the ground that the time for completion of the 
project has been extended upto 30.09.2026 and therefore the 
application under Order 21 Rule 54 of the Code of Civil 
Procedure has no legal basis. However he failed to advance 
any lawful explanation as to why the said application lacks 
legal foundation. Such submission appears to be devoid of 
merit and cannot be accepted.  
In the above view of the matter this Court finds that the 
executing Court has rightly passed the impugned judgment 
and order in accordance with law and no illegality or infirmity 

<<PAGE 13>>
 
13
can be found therein. Although the impugned judgment was 
not delivered with detailed analysis nevertheless no failure of 
justice has been occasioned thereby.  
On the foregoing analysis the impugned judgment does 
not call for interference. The petitioner has failed to 
substantiate his claim or to establish any legal ground 
warranting interference by this Court.  
Accordingly the Rule being devoid of merit is 
discharged.  
Communicate this judgment to the concerned Court at 
once.  
 
 
Md. Ali Reza, J: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Naher-B.O
input_summary: Owning 50 decimals of urban land, OPPOSITE PARTIES contracted in October 2004 with developer PETITIONER for a 15-storied building; after 2016 arbitration proceedings under the Arbitration Act, 2001, a 2021 compromise yielded a March 2022 consent award. Alleging overdue completion, OPPOSITE PARTIES brought a 2024 execution case for accrued rent and secured an Order 21 Rule 54 Code of Civil Procedure attachment of PETITIONER's share on 20.03.2025. Under a May 2025 revisional stay requiring payment of one-third arrear rent within 30 days, PETITIONER tendered Tk. 14,08,800 against OPPOSITE PARTIES' one-third figure of Tk. 1,69,05,600 out of Tk. 5,07,16,800 for 40,830 sq. ft. commercial space and 32 flats. PETITIONER alleged an unnotified, non-speaking, disproportionate attachment against a Tk. 42,26,400 claim, delivered flats, and a developers' association extension to September 2026.
explanation: Noting the 02.03.2022 compromise award was enforceable as a civil decree under Section 44 of the Arbitration Act 2001, the Court held attachment of immovable property under Order 21 Rule 54 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 is a preventive measure restraining alienation without dispossession and requires no prior monetary valuation of the attached share. Execution notices were duly served, PETITIONER willfully breached the conditional stay by depositing only Tk. 14,08,800 instead of one-third (Tk. 1,69,05,600) of Tk. 5,07,16,800 arrears, and a private developers' association circular could not render execution premature.

input_summary: OPPOSITE PARTY instituted a 2016 civil suit against PETITIONER seeking invalidation of an instrument, which PETITIONER contested as defendant; on 06.06.2021, OPPOSITE PARTY obtained a trial decree. Challenging that decree, PETITIONER preferred a 2021 title appeal before the Senior District Judge. When the appeal came up for hearing on 13.07.2023, PETITIONER's application seeking an adjournment failed and the appeal was terminated for non-appearance. On 16.07.2023—within the prescribed limitation period—PETITIONER applied under Order 41 Rule 19A of the Code of Civil Procedure for readmission of the appeal, which the appellate court turned down on 21.04.2024. Obtaining a revisional Rule on 11.06.2024, PETITIONER remained unrepresented at hearing, whereas counsel for OPPOSITE PARTY appeared and expressed no objection to PETITIONER's revisional plea on the ground that statutory law favoured readmission.
explanation: Examining the revisional record upon hearing OPPOSITE PARTY's counsel—who candidly conceded that the law supported PETITIONER's readmission plea—the Court held that since PETITIONER's application of 16.07.2023 to readmit the appeal terminated on 13.07.2023 had been filed within time, turning it down on 21.04.2024 contravened Order 41 Rule 19A of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908. Vacating the impugned appellate order, the Court directed the appellate court to dispose of the appeal expeditiously, preferably within six months, without permitting adjournments absent extreme necessity.

The opposite parties as plaintiff filed the instant Title

Banaripara for declaration of title which was dismissed on 
20.09.1993. Plaintiffs then preferred Title Appeal Number 272 
of 1993 and in appeal amended the plaint for partition and the 
suit was sent down on remand on 22.04.1996. The suit was 
then decreed in preliminary form on 27.02.1997. Thereafter 
plaintiffs prayed for appointment of Advocate Commissioner 
named Amzad Hossain who filed report on 15.06.1998. None 
filed objection against that report. Decree was made final on 
26.04.2005 pursuant to order dated 17.04.2005 and plaintiffs

The petitioners being defendants 1-2 preferred Title 
Appeal 75 of 1997 against the preliminary decree dated

Defendants then preferred Civil Revision 2278 of 1998 which 
was discharged on 20.07.2002. Against which they preferred

another Title Suit 82 of 2012 which was dismissed on contest

preferred at the instance of the plaintiffs also failed on 
05.09.2021.

on 10.05.2010 plaintiffs filed the instant Title Appeal 110 of 
2021 on 21.11.2021 which was allowed by the impugned 
judgment and decree dated 12.09.2022.

Mr. Md. Nasir Uddin appearing on behalf of the petitioners 
submits that the instant appeal was filed after 11 years of the 
decree and as such the same is barred by limitation but the 
appellate Court did not advert to this important aspect of the 
case thus committed error of law resulting in an error in such 
decree occasioning failure of justice. He then submits that the 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
instant appeal is barred by Section 11 of the Code of Civil 
Procedure because plaintiff earlier failed in Title Suit Number 
82 of 2012 as well as in Title Appeal Number 31 of 2018 
where the subject-matter and matter in issue between the 
parties were same. He contends that the dispute ended in 
Execution Case 05 of 2010 by which possession was delivered 
and the appellate Court failed to appreciate that dismissal of 
judgment and decree dated 10.05.2010 does not mean that the 
execution also ended thus committed error of law occasioning 
failure of justice. He finally submits that since there is merit in 
the Rule the impugned judgment and decree may be interfered 
with.  
On the other hand learned Advocate Mr. Syed Nafiul 
Islam appearing on behalf of the opposite parties most 
emphatically submits that the appellate Court committed no 
error of law resulting in an error in such decree occasioning 
failure of justice in allowing the appeal and the appellate 
Court delivered the judgment with great circumspection. He 
submits that the appellate Court decided in favour of taking all 
steps which were legally required to preserve equity in 
accordance with the principles and provisions of the law of 
partition. He then contends that since the judgment of the 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5

partition and allotment among the parties the judgment of the 
appellate Court is legally sustainable and acceptable. He 
points out that the impugned judgment having been passed by 
following the law of equity and justice any interference by the 
revisional Court would result in a failure of justice. He finally 
submits that as the Rule is devoid of merit the same is liable to 
be discharged.  
Heard the learned Advocates for both sides and perused 
the materials on record and also gone through the impugned 
judgments passed by the Courts below. 
The fact of the case reveals that the litigation between 
the parties commenced as far back as the year 1993. The 
opposite parties as plaintiff initially filed Title Suit 01 of 1993 
seeking declaration of title. The said suit was dismissed on 
20.09.1993. Being aggrieved plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal 
272 of 1993 wherein the plaint was amended converting the 
relief into one for partition. The appellate Court allowed the 
amendment and remanded the suit by judgment and order 
dated 22.04.1996.  

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
Upon remand the suit proceeded and a preliminary 
decree was passed on 27.02.1997 determining the share of the 
plaintiffs.  
The present petitioners who were defendants 1-2 
challenged the present decree by filing Title Appeal 75 of 
1997. The appeal was dismissed on 12.04.1998. Thereafter the 
defendants approached this Court by filing Civil Revision 
2278 of 1998 which was ultimately discharged on 20.07.2002.  
Defendants then filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal 
1896 of 2002 before the Honourable Appellate Division. By 
judgment dated 30.06.2003 the Appellate Division directed 
allotment of saham measuring 82.50 decimals of land in 
favour of the defendants.  
The said judgment attained finality and became binding 
upon the parties under Article 111 of the Constitution and 
Section 97 of the Code of Civil Procedure.  
In compliance with the direction of the Appellate 
Division an Advocate Commissioner was appointed. On the 
basis of the report of the Commissioner a final decree was 
passed on 10.05.2010.  

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
The defendants thereafter initiated Execution Case 05 of 
2010 and obtained delivery of possession through Court on 
10.06.2012. The case was finally disposed of on 23.09.2012.  
Thus the decree was not only attained finality but was 
fully executed and satisfied.  
Despite the execution of the final decree the plaintiffs 
filed another Title Suit 82 of 2012 challenging the decree. The 
suit was dismissed on 19.02.2018.  
The appeal preferred therefrom being Title Appeal 31 of 
2018 was also dismissed on 05.09.2021.  
However in a glaring abuse of process plaintiffs again 
filed Title Appeal 110 of 2021 on 21.11.2021 challenging the 
final decree dated 10.05.2010 after lapse of more than 11 
years.  
The appellate Court entertained the appeal without 
addressing the bar of limitation and allowed the same which 
has given rise to the present revision.  
Section 96 of the Code of Civil Procedure confers a 
substantive right to prefer an appeal from every decree passed 
by court exercising original jurisdiction. Order 41 of the Code 
prescribes the procedural methods regulating the filing and 
hearing and disposal of such appeals.  

<<PAGE 8>>
 
8
However the exercise of appellate jurisdiction is subject 
to the law of limitation which is mandatory and jurisdictional.  
Section 97 of the Code lays down a fundamental 
principle that where a party aggrieved by a preliminary decree 
does not appeal therefrom he shall be precluded from 
disputing its correctness in any appeal preferred from the final 
decree.  
The limitation for filing an appeal from a decree is 
governed by the Limitation Act, 1908. Under Article 152 of 
the First Schedule the prescribed period for filing an appeal 
from a decree is 30 days from the date of the decree.  
The final decree in the present case was passed on 
10.05.2010. Even after excluding the date of decree and the 
time requisite for obtaining certified copies as contemplated 
under Section 12 of the Limitation Act the appeal ought to 
have been filed within 30 days.  
The appeal was however filed on 21.11.2021 after lapse 
of more than 11 years.  
Section 5 of the Limitation Act empowers the Court to 
condone the delay upon sufficient cause but no such 
application was shown to have been filed and entertained by 

<<PAGE 9>>
 
9
the appellate Court. In absence of such application the 
appellate Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the appeal.   
Limitation does not merely bar the remedy but 
extinguishes the jurisdiction of the Court to entertain a time 
barred appeal.  
A final decree is the formal expression of an 
adjudication which so far as regards the Court expressing it 
conclusively determines the rights of the parties with regard to 
all or any of the matters in controversy in the suit and is 
executable unless stayed or set aside by a competent court.  
In the present case the final decree was not only passed 
but fully executed and possession was delivered through court. 
Once a decree has been executed and satisfaction recorded the 
rights of the parties stand crystallized.  
Reopening such decree after a decade defeats the 
doctrine of finality with certainty and repose which are 
foundational to civil adjudication.  
The appellate Court failed to address the bar under 
Article 152 of the Limitation Act. It ignored the mandatory 
requirement of Section 5 of the Limitation Act. It overlooked 
Section 97 of the Code of Civil Procedure and interfered with 
a decree which had long attained finality and stood executed. 

<<PAGE 10>>
 
10
Such omission amounts to a jurisdictional error and error of 
law resulting in an error in such decree occasioning failure of 
justice with material irregularity in exercise of jurisdiction 
warranting interference under Section 115(1) of the Code of 
Civil Procedure. The appeal was hopelessly barred by 
limitation.  
In the result the Rule is made absolute.  
The impugned judgment and decree dated 12.09.2022 
passed in Title Appeal 110 of 2021 are set aside.  
The final decree dated 10.05.2010 together with the 
execution proceedings and delivery of possession are 
affirmed.  
 The order of status quo passed by this Court stands 
vacated.  
Communicate this judgment to the concerned Court and 
send down the lower Courts’ record.  
 
 
Md. Ali Reza, J: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Naher-B.O

explanation: Applying Article 152 and Sections 5 and 12 of the Limitation Act 1908 alongside Section 97 of the Code of Civil Procedure and Article 111 of the Constitution, the Court held an appeal against the 10.05.2010 final decree had to be filed within thirty days, and entertaining an appeal filed over eleven years later on 21.11.2021 without any Section 5 condonation petition exceeded appellate jurisdiction. defendant 1 and in an attempt to obtain relief from the said 
criminal proceeding defendant 1 executed an affidavit on 

<<PAGE 17>>
 
17
31.05.2006 Exhibit-9 before notary public wherein she 
categorically stated that she neither claimed nor had ever 
claimed any right or title or interest in the suit land on the 
basis of Exhibit-7 nor would she do so in future and she had 
no objection if the said deed was cancelled. The judgment

were subsequently dispossessed therefrom by the defendants. 
Although the issues of possession and dispossession were 
incidentally and unnecessarily referred to in Exhibit-8 no such 
allegation was ever made by the plaintiffs in the said criminal 
case instituted under the aforesaid sections of the Penal Code 
which do not relate to criminal trespass. In the present case 
plaintiffs made out a definite case that they were dispossessed 
on 25.11.2009 and the statement in Exhibit-8 on dispossession 
is merely the statement of the investigating officer and not that 

<<PAGE 18>>
 
18
of the plaintiffs as claimed either in the criminal case or in the 
present case.  
In paragraph 6 of the plaint the plaintiffs have clearly 
and categorically stated that on 25.11.2009 at about 5 P.M. 
they were forcibly dispossessed from the suit land. It is also 
stated that on 29.05.2010 when plaintiffs demanded 
restoration of possession on last occasion the defendant 
refused such demand and asserted title on the basis of the deed 
mentioned in schedule-Kha. Thereafter on 06.06.2010 the 
plaintiffs upon obtaining the certified copy of the said deed 
filed the present suit. From Exhibit-7 it evidently appears that 
the certified copy of the said deed was also obtained on the 
same date which fully corresponds with the date of accrual of 
the cause of action as stated in the plaint. Moreover defendant 
1 while examined as DW 1 has explicitly stated during cross-
examination that she has no objection if Exhibit-7 is cancelled 
by an order of the Court. From the entire sequence of events it 
is apparent that defendant with an oblique motive has been 
unlawfully harassing the plaintiffs for a considerable period 
with the intent to wrongfully grab and appropriate the suit 
land.  

<<PAGE 19>>
 
19
Defendant 1 claims that she has title and possession in 
8.5 decimals of land in the suit plots including 4 decimals of 
land by purchase from the common vendor Jabbar and 
accordingly produced the purchase deeds Exhibits Thha and 
Da. Exhibits Ka series and Kha series also show that she is the 
R.S. recorded tenant and has been paying rent in respect of 8.5 
decimals of land. As discussed above defendant 1 has not 
claimed any interest in the suit land by dint of Exhibit-7 and 
thus it is clear that the 8.5 decimals of land belonging to 
defendant 1 does not in any way attract the suit land or affect 
the interest of the plaintiffs over the suit land.   
It has already been discussed and found that plaintiffs 
have title and possession in the suit land and the defendant has 
title and possession in respect of her own share measuring 
eight and a half decimals in R.S. plot numbers 1610 and 1611. 
PW 2 who is the son of Jabbar corroborated PW 1 and stated 
in his deposition that on 25.11.2009 Wednesday plaintiffs 
were forcibly dispossessed from the suit land. It is a matter of 
great legal significance that no cross-examination whatsoever 
was conducted by the defendant challenging or disputing this 
material and vital statement of PW 2. Such non-denial 
amounts to admission and in view of Section 58 of the 

<<PAGE 20>>
 
20
Evidence Act a strong presumption arises in favour of the 
truth of the said unchallenged statement. On the other hand 
from a careful reading of the deposition of DW 1 it does not 
appear to have disclosed any specific denial by her against the 
case of dispossession of the plaintiffs.  
Plaintiffs have further asserted that defendant earlier 
filed Title Suit 195 of 1999 claiming title over the disputed 
land on the basis of the same disputed deed Exhibit-7. Upon 
dismissal of the said suit defendant preferred Title Appeal 
Number 127 of 2004. During pendency of the appeal 
defendant forcibly dispossessed the plaintiffs from the suit 
land and subsequently withdrew the appeal on 24.02.2010 as 
evident from Exhibit-10. DW 1 during her cross-examination 
admitted that she filed Title Suit 195 of 1999 against plaintiff 
1 with regard to the suit land which was dismissed and the 
appeal against such dismissal was withdrawn by her. Thus 
from a combined reading of the statement of plaint and 
admission made by DW 1 along with Exhibit-10 it becomes 
evident that defendant previously made repeated attempts both 
before civil and criminal Courts to wrongfully appropriate the 
suit land but failed in all such attempts.  

<<PAGE 21>>
 
21
The RS record 3122 Exhibit-Ka approves that the said 
khatian was prepared in the name of the defendant showing an 
area of 7.50 decimals of land. From the schedule of the plaint 
and Exhibit-3 it is clearly established that plaintiffs were 
dispossessed from 3 decimals of land out of RS plot 1610. 
DW 1 has admitted that she is in possession of a total area of 
16.75 decimals under the suit khatian. This admission clearly 
indicates that the defendant is in possession of land in excess 
of her lawful share of eight and a half decimals.  
The only reasonable inference from the above facts is 
that although the defendant formally denied Exhibit-7 but she 
nevertheless relied upon the foundation of the said forged deed 
at a later point of time and in the year 2009 wrongfully denied 
the title of the plaintiffs and forcibly dispossessed them from 
the suit land.  
Therefore upon a comprehensive consideration of the 
evidence on record it explicitly appears that plaintiffs have 
successfully proved their title and also case of possession 
followed by dispossession in the suit land and also their case 
of cancellation of Exhibit-7 which cannot be left outstanding.  
Learned Advocate for the petitioner Mr. Chowdhury 
with much ingenuity referred to Exhibit-8 and Exhibit-Gha 

<<PAGE 22>>
 
22
and submitted that since the plaintiffs had instituted a criminal 
case in the year 1999 challenging Exhibit-7 and since the 
police report directly or incidentally mentioned the issue of 
possession and dispossession in the year 1999 the present suit 
filed in 2010 is barred by limitation. He further argued that in 
the present suit the reliefs of declaration of title and 
cancellation of deed are substantive reliefs and as such both 
are barred under Article 120 and Article 91 of the Limitation 
Act. On that ground he contended that no decree could legally 
be passed in the present suit. He did not put forward any reply 
on the question as to why the relief of recovery of possession 
could not be the substantive relief. He also contended that the 
trial Court committed an error of law by delivering the 
impugned judgment without framing any specific issue on 
limitation and without recording and finding thereon rendering 
the judgment unsustainable in the eye of law. In support of his 
submissions Mr. Chowdhury relied upon the cases of ANMW 
Nobi and another Vs. Md. Bolai Roy and others reported in 15 
BLT(AD) 27 and Hamida Begum Vs. Fayez Ahmed reported 
in 77 DLR(HD) 108. Exhibit-8 and Exhibit-Gha along with 
the pleadings and other relevant evidence on record have 
already been discussed in detail hereinbefore. Upon such 

<<PAGE 23>>
 
23
consideration this Court has clearly arrived at the finding that 
the plaintiffs filed the instant suit well within the prescribed 
period of limitation reckoning from the date of accrual of the 
cause of action as pleaded in the plaint. Therefore even if no 
specific issue on limitation was framed no prejudice has been 
caused to the defendant in the trial of the suit. Moreover had 
such an issue been framed the result would have remained the 
same in view of the facts and evidence on record. It also calls 
for attention that defendant did not raise any question in 
respect of raising such issue in appeal. Therefore the 
principles laid down in 15 BLT and 77 DLR cases are not 
applicable considering the facts and circumstances of the 
present case which are wholly distinct and materially different. 
Mr. Chowdhury further submitted that since the present 
suit is filed against co-sharer the same is not maintainable in 
its present form without seeking partition of the joint property. 
In support of this contention he referred to the cases of Sabiha 
Khanam Vs. Jaitun Bibi and others reported in 3 BLC(AD) 
175; Jahangir Alam Vs. Shabdir Ahmed and others reported in 
22 BLC(AD) 75. As already discussed earlier the plaintiffs 
have clearly proved that from the year 1970 and through all 
subsequent transactions culminating in the deeds marked as 

<<PAGE 24>>
 
24
Exhibits 4, 5 series and 6 series the suit land has been 
transferred with specific and definite boundaries. The same 
boundaries of Exhibits 4, 5 series and 6 series have been 
described in the schedule of the plaint and accordingly 
possession has been asserted over a clearly identified and 
demarcated portion of land. Since the plaintiffs have filed the 
instant suit against the defendant-co-sharer with respect to a 
specifically demarcated portion of land with defined 
boundaries there remains no legal bar to the maintainability of 
the present suit without a prayer for partition. Accordingly for 
the reasons stated above the precedents of 3 BLC and 22 BLC 
cases relied upon by Mr. Chowdhury are not applicable to the 
facts and circumstances of the present case.  
Petitioner raised the question of remand upon absolutely 
frivolous grounds. Remand cannot be granted as a matter of 
course. Remand of a suit for fresh trial should not be ordered 
on mere technicalities or flimsy grounds. Remand should not 
be lightly made if the evidence on record is sufficient for the 
Court to decide the question itself. Order of remand of a case 
for fresh hearing when there is sufficient evidence on record 
tantamounts to shirking the responsibility affecting the course 
of justice. No remand order can be passed to give an 

<<PAGE 25>>
 
25
opportunity to a party to fill up the lacuna in his or her case. 
Considering the facts and circumstances of the present case 
and the overall discussions I find no substance in the 
application for remand filed on 15.07.2025 and hence the 
application is rejected.  
In view of the foregoing discussions, findings and 
reasons this Court finds no merit in this Rule.  
Accordingly the Rule is discharged. The judgment and 
decree passed by both the Courts below are hereby affirmed.     
The order of stay passed by this Court stands vacated.  
Communicate this judgment to the concerned Court and 
send down the lower Courts’ record.  
 
 
Md. Ali Reza, J: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Naher-B.O
