judgment_text:
<<PAGE 1>>
Bench: 
Mr. Justice Md. Ali Reza 
 
Civil Revision No. 196 of 2014 
 
Md. Abul Kalam 
         ......petitioner  
                              -Versus- 
Md. Sahidullah and others 
                                              ......opposite parties  
       
Mr. Mohammed Mutahar Hossain with 
Mr. Rashed Ahmed Rishat and 
Mr. Saimon Islam, Advocates  
 
 
               ......for the petitioner  
 
Mr. Md. Abdul Haque, Senior Advocate with 
Ms. Shahanara Jaman Santa, Advocate 
 
 
 
 
......for the opposite parties 
 
Heard on: 08.01.2026, 28.01.2026, 
03.02.2026, 10.02.2026 and 18.02.2026 
 
Judgment on: 25.02.2026 
 
 
 
In the instant revision Rule was issued calling upon the 
opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned 
judgment and decree dated 30.06.2013 passed by the learned 
Additional District Judge, 4th Court, Mymensingh in Other 
Appeal No. 206 of 2004 allowing the appeal and affirming the 
judgment and decree dated 11.08.2004 passed by the learned 
Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Mymensingh in other Class 
Suit No. 06 of 2003 decreeing the suit should not be set aside 
and/or such other or further order or orders be passed as to this 
Court may seem fit and proper.  

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
Petitioner as defendant filed Other Suit Number 28 of 
2000 in the Court of Session Judge, 2nd Court, Mymensingh 
on 23.07.2000 which was subsequently transferred to the 
Court of Session Judge, 3rd Court, Mymensing and 
renumbered as Other Suit Number 06 of 2003 and the suit was 
filed for enforcement of contract dated 23.02.1998.  
The case of the plaintiff is that the suit land appertaining 
to the schedule of the plaint belonged to defendant 1. During 
the subsistence of financial distress defendant expressed his 
intention to sell the suit land and accordingly on 23.02.1998 
plaintiff agreed to purchase the same in presence of local 
witnesses. The consideration was fixed at Tk. 1,20,000/- (one 
lac twenty thousand) out of which plaintiff paid Tk. 75,000/- 
(seventy five thousand) to defendant as earnest money and 
defendant executed and delivered an agreement for sale in 
favour of the plaintiff acknowledging receipt of the said 
amount. It was stipulated in the contract that within 06(six) 
months from 23.02.1998 defendant would receive the balance 
consideration and execute and register a kabala deed in favour 
of the plaintiff. Plaintiff within 04(four) months from the date 
of the agreement tendered the remaining Tk. 45,000/- (forty 
five thousand) and repeatedly requested the defendant to 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
execute and register the sale deed but defendant on various 
pleas including alleged family disputes avoided performance 
and assured that after settlement of such disputes he would 
accept the balance consideration and execute and register the 
deed. Subsequently in a local arbitration held on 09.01.2000 at 
the house of the defendant in presence of local elites the 
defendant admitted the execution of the agreement and receipt 
of earnest money and agreed to execute and register the sale 
deed. However in disregard of the decision of the arbitration 
defendant refused to accept the balance consideration and to 
execute and register the deed on 09.07.2000. Hence the suit.  
Defendant 1 filed written statement on 17.09.2001 
denying the material averments made in the plaint. In 
substance defendant contended that the suit land originally 
belonged to his father and upon his death devolved upon the 
defendant and other heirs. Defendant denied having executed 
any agreement in favour of the plaintiff or having received Tk. 
75,000/- (seventy five thousand) as alleged. Plaintiff actually 
has forged the signature shown to have been executed by the 
defendant in the agreement by copying the signature of 
defendant from gift deed dated 03.09.1996 executed by him in 
favour of the mother of the plaintiff. It is further contended 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
that plaintiff taking advantage of prior acquaintance and 
enmity manufactured this false and forged agreement showing 
execution by the defendant. The alleged document is described 
as written on non-judicial stamp and purportedly attested by 
interested witnesses. The defendant asserted that he never 
appeared before any scribe for execution of such document 
nor did he receive any earnest money from the plaintiff. The 
alleged agreement is forged and fabricated and the plaintiff by 
producing interested witnesses has attempted to create false 
claim. Defendant denied the holding of any arbitration as 
alleged by the plaintiff. It is further stated that when plaintiff 
attempted to interfere with the possession of the defendant on 
20.09.2000 defendant then lodged Criminal Case Number 
2828 of 2000 under Sections 467/468/471/109 of the Penal 
Code before the Court of Magistrate and he further filed 
General Diary bearing Entry Number 890 dated 23.09.2000 
stating that the plaintiff’s allegations are false and concocted. 
The suit being false is liable to be dismissed. 
Trial Court framed as many as five issues. During course 
of trial plaintiff examined 06 witnesses and defendant 1 
examined 04 witnesses. Plaintiff adduced the agreement dated 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
23.02.1998 which was marked in evidence as Exhibit-1. 
Defendant adduced no document.  
Trial Court upon perusal of the pleadings and hearing the 
parties and considering both oral and documentary evidence 
decreed the suit by judgment and decree dated 11.08.2004. As 
against the same defendant preferred Other Appeal Number 
206 of 2004 before the Court of District Judge, Mymensingh 
which on transfer was heard by Additional District Judge, 4th 
Court, Mymensingh who was pleased to dismiss the same by 
judgment and decree dated 30.06.2013. Feeling aggrieved by 
the judgments passed by the Cours below defendant filed this 
revision and obtained Rule on 20.01.2014.  
Learned Advocate Mohammed Mutahar Hossain along 
with Mr. Rashed Ahmed Rishat appearing on behalf of the 
defendant-petitioner submits that the Courts below wrongly 
shifted the onus upon the defendant to prove that the alleged 
signature shown to have been given by the defendant in the 
agreement is forged and not of the defendant violating the 
settled principle of law that plaintiff has to prove his own case 
and under the law burden of proof was never discharged by 
the plaintiff thus the Courts below committed error of law 
resulting in an error in such decree occasioning failure of 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
justice. He submits that plaintiff was not ready and willing to 
perform his part of the contract as apparent from the judgment 
passed by the trial Court where it has been ordered that within 
30(thirty) days from the decree the rest amount would be 
deposited in the Court and the same has been violated as 
apparent from reading of the record of the Court. He submits 
that plaintiff failed to prove the alleged contents of and 
signature on the agreement as genuine thus the Courts 
committed error of law occasioning failure of justice. 
Referring to Exhibit-1 he contends that the time fixed for 
performance was 06(six) months but plaintiff remained silent 
for a long time and did not produce any independent and 
corroborative evidence to show that he has tendered the rest 
amount of the consideration within the stipulated time and 
both the Courts below failed to consider this aspect of the case 
and also that an unregistered agreement should be dealt with 
extreme caution thus the Courts below committed error of law 
occasioning failure of justice. He also refers to the case of 
Roshanally Vs. Zakir Hossain reported in 16 BLC 85 and 
submits that Exhibit-1 is not executable being unilateral 
document and possession was not delivered to the plaintiff 
pursuant to such agreement. He further refers to the ratio laid 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
down in AIR 2008 SC 1541 case and submits that as a matter 
of extreme caution and judicial sobriety the Court should not 
normally take upon itself the responsibility of comparing the 
disputed signature with that of the admitted signature and in 
the event of slightest doubt leave the matter to the wisdom of 
experts. He points out that the Courts below committed error 
of law occasioning failure of justice in examining and 
comparing the disputed signature in cursory manner on the 
basis of a mere casual or routine glance or perusal which is 
hazardous and risky without resorting to scientific method. He 
then submits that the Courts below failed to appreciate that 
since the suit land is a joint property and the title is under 
dispute the Court should not exercise its discretionary power 
to grant equitable relief in a suit for specific performance of 
contract. He then contends that the Courts below committed 
error of law occasioning failure of justice in ignoring the 
material fact that the disputed signature was a product of 
forgery done on the basis of the signature given by defendant 
1 in gift deed dated 03.09.1996. He finally submits that the 
impugned judgments being perverse and misconceived are 
liable to be set aside and prays that the Rule having merit may 
be made absolute.   

<<PAGE 8>>
 
8
On the other hand learned Senior Advocate Mr. Md. 
Abdul Haque along with Ms. shahanara Jaman Santa 
appearing on behalf of plaintiff-opposite party 1 taking 
through the evidence on record submits that the plaintiff’s 
acceptance of the defendant’s proposal for transfer of the suit 
land and the fixation of the consideration money along with 
the payment of earnest money to the defendant have been 
satisfactorily proved by the oral and documentary evidence 
adduced by the plaintiff. He contends that the trial Court upon 
proper appreciation of evidence on record rightly decreed the 
suit and the appellate Court upon independent assessment in 
strict compliance with Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil 
Procedure affirmed the said decree assigning precise and 
reasoned findings. Since the Courts below did not commit any 
error of law occasioning failure of justice the impugned 
judgments are immune from interference. Referring to 
Sections 101, 102 and 103 of the Evidence Act he submits that 
the burden of proof as to any particular fact lies upon the 
person who desires the Court to believe in the existence of that 
fact. According to him the plaintiff having discharged his 
initial onus under Section 101 of the Evidence Act by proving 
the agreement and payment of earnest money the burden 

<<PAGE 9>>
 
9
shifted upon the defendant to establish that the disputed 
signature was not that of the defendant. He further contends 
that the proposition that an unregistered agreement for sale 
must necessarily be signed by both parties failing which a 
unilateral document becomes unenforceable is unsupported by 
any statutory provision. He also submits that the decisions 
cited by the petitioner are distinguishable on facts and are not 
applicable to the present case in view of the pleadings and 
evidence on record. Finally he submits that no material 
illegality or irregularity or jurisdictional error having been 
demonstrated the impugned judgments are not amenable to 
interference in revision under Section 115(1) of the Code of 
Civil Procedure and accordingly the Rule being devoid of 
merit is liable to be discharged.  
Heard the learned Advocates for both sides and perused 
the materials on record and also gone through the impugned 
judgments passed by the courts below. 
This is a suit for specific performance of contract. The 
contract in question was executed on 23.02.1998 and has been 
marked as Exhibit-1. The time fixed for performance under 
Exhibit-1 is 06(six) months. On perusal of paragraphs 3, 4 and 
5 of the plaint it transpires that within the stipulated period 

<<PAGE 10>>
 
10
plaintiff tendered the balance consideration money but 
defendant on the plea of family complications requested for 
time and assured that he would execute and register the sale 
deed subsequently. But when defendant later disclosed his 
intention to transfer the land to his brother a local arbitration 
was held on 09.07.2000 in presence of local respectable 
persons wherein defendant admitted execution of the 
agreement and receipt of earnest money. Nevertheless 
defendant failed to perform his obligation under the contract 
and on 09.07.2000 refused to execute and register the deed in 
terms of the agreement. Thereafter the plaintiff instituted the 
present suit on 23.07.2000.  
On the other hand as appears from paragraph 8 of the 
written statement the definite case of the defendant is that he 
never executed any such agreement. He asserts that by a 
registered deed dated 03.09.1996 he transferred 25 decimals of 
land in favour of plaintiff’s mother and the said deed remains 
in the custody of the plaintiff. According to defendant out of 
enmity and with an intention to grab his land plaintiff copied 
the signature appearing in the said registered deed and thereby 
manufactured the unregistered agreement in question.  

<<PAGE 11>>
 
11
In support of the plaintiff’s case PW 1 has been 
corroborated by PW 2 to PW 6. PW 2 deposed that he is an 
attesting witness to agreement and after negotiation plaintiff 
brought money from PW 4 and through PW 6 got Exhibit-1 
written whereupon defendant received Tk. 75,000/- (seventy 
five) as earnest money and signed the document Exhibit-1. 
PW 3 stated that after the consideration of Tk. 1,20,000/- (one 
lac twenty thousand) was settled at the plaintiff’s house the 
defendant demanded money and the parties went to 
Mymensingh to collect the money from PW 4 and thereafter 
Exhibit-1 was written by PW 6 at the Sub-Registry Office and 
defendant upon receipt of Tk. 75,000/- (seventy five thousand) 
signed the same. PW 4 stated that at the time of payment of 
Tk. 75,000/- (seventy five thousand) the defendant, PW 3 and 
others were present. PW 5 corroborated that the plaintiff’s 
money was kept with PW 4. PW 6 a deed writer of 
Mymensingh Sub-Registry Office deposed that Exhibit-1was 
written by him as per instructions of the executant and the 
transaction of Tk. 75,000/- (seventy five thousand) took place 
in his presence.  
The consistent testimony PW 2 to PW 6 corroborating 
PW 1 on material particulars has not been effectively shaken 

<<PAGE 12>>
 
12
in cross-examination. The plaintiff has thus proved Exhibit-1 
through the attesting witnesses and the scribe in accordance 
with law.  
Conversely DW 1 stated that the plaintiff forged the 
agreement by imitating his signature from the registered deed 
dated 03.09.1996. In cross-examination he admitted that the 
signature appearing in the agreement resembled his signature 
though he denied having signed it.  
In such a circumstance an important aspect deserves 
specific mention. The definite case of the defendant is that the 
bainapatra was forged by copying his signature from a 
registered deed dated 03.09.1996. That document constitutes 
the very foundation of the defence plea of forgery. Yet the 
defendant neither produced the original deed nor any certified 
copy thereof. In terms of Sections 61-65 of the Evidence Act 
contents of a document must be proved by primary evidence 
except in cases where secondary evidence is admissible. 
Furthermore procedural remedies were available to the 
defendant under Order 11 Rule 14 of the Code of Civil 
Procedure to compel production of the document if allegedly 
in possession of the plaintiff and under Order 16 Rule 6 of the 
Code of Civil Procedure to summon the document from the 

<<PAGE 13>>
 
13
Sub-Registry Office. No such steps were taken. In absence of 
proof of the 1996 deed the plea that the signature was imitated 
from that deed remains wholly unsubstantiated. In this context 
the submission that it was the plaintiff’s duty to obtain expert 
opinion is entirely misconceived. The plaintiff having proved 
execution of Exhibit-1 through attesting witnesses and the 
scribe and payment of earnest money and the admitted 
signatures being available for comparison under Section 73 of 
the Evidence Act his initial burden under Section 101 stands 
discharged. The specific allegation of forgery having been 
raised by the defendant the burden under Section 103 of the 
Evidence Act squarely lies upon him to prove that allegation. 
Since the defence case entirely depends upon the existence 
and genuineness of the alleged deed of 03.09.1996 failure to 
produce and prove that document renders the defence plea 
legally unsustainable. In such circumstances no adverse 
inference can be drawn against the plaintiff for not producing 
expert evidence.  
Another significant circumstance deserves mention. PW 
2 and PW 3 stated in cross-examination that the stamp used in 
the agreement was brought from the defendant’s house. 
Exhibit-1 itself shows that the stamp was purchased in the 

<<PAGE 14>>
 
14
name of the defendant. This circumstance leads to a 
reasonable inference that defendant purchased the stamp in his 
own name and executed the agreement upon receipt of Tk. 
75,000/- (seventy five thousand) as earnest money.  
Moreover so far as the transaction of earnest money is 
concerned the evidence of PW 2, PW 3 and PW 4 fully 
corroborates PW 1 on material particulars. No material 
discrepancy or contradiction or inconsistency has been 
detected in their cross-examination. Each of them has 
consistently supported the other regarding negotiation, 
settlement of consideration, bringing of stamp, writing of the 
bainapatra and payment of Tk. 75,000/- (seventy five 
thousand) as earnest money. Their evidence are natural, 
consistent and mutually corroborative and therefore inspire 
confidence.  
With regard to the signature appearing on Exhibit-1 the 
same has been compared with the admitted signatures of the 
defendant appearing on the Vokalatnama dated 22.10.2000, 
the written statement dated 17.09.2001 and the signatures 
appended by him after giving deposition before the Court on 
27.01.2004 and 31.05.2004. On a careful side-by-side 
comparison it is evident that the signatures bearing the name 

<<PAGE 15>>
 
15
“Md. Abul Kalam” on all these documents are substantially 
similar and appear to have been written by one and the same 
person. The formation of letters and the manner of 
commencement with termination strokes, pen pressure pattern, 
alignment, slant, proportion between letters, spacing and 
characteristic fluency disclose common authorship. The 
natural variations noticed are minor and fall within the 
permissible range of individual variation recognized in 
forensic handwriting analysis. Such slight divergence does not 
indicate fabrication but rather supports genuineness since 
exact uniformity is often symptomatic of simulation. It is 
neither abnormal nor legally suspicious that a person’s 
signature may slightly vary depending upon physical 
condition, writing speed, writing surface, surrounding 
circumstances or mental state at the time of signing.     
When Sections 45, 47, 67 and 73 of the Evidence Act are 
read conjointly the legal position becomes clear. Section 67 
requires proof of signature or handwriting of the person 
alleged to have signed the document. Section 47 renders 
relevancy of the opinion of a person acquainted with such 
handwriting. Section 45 makes expert opinion relevant but not 
conclusive. Section 73 empowers the Court itself to compare 

<<PAGE 16>>
 
16
disputed handwriting with admitted handwriting. The 
combined effect of these provisions is that expert opinion is 
merely advisory and not binding. The Court is competent to 
form its own conclusion upon comparison particularly where 
there exists direct evidence of execution by attesting witnesses 
and the scribe. Therefore in presence of reliable evidence and 
admitted signatures available for comparison absence of 
expert evidence does not render the plaintiff’s case defective 
nor is expert evidence infallible or decisive.  
The appellate Court having undertaken comparison of 
signatures in exercise of power under Section 73 of the 
Evidence Act and having assigned cogent reasons its finding 
regarding genuineness of signature is a finding of fact based 
on evidence and does not call for interference.  
The submission of the learned Advocate for the 
petitioner that complicated question of title is involved and 
therefore decree ought not to have been passed is 
misconceived. The present suit is not one for declaration of 
title but a suit for specific performance of contract governed 
by the Specific Relief Act. In such a suit the Court is 
concerned with existence of a valid contract along with 
passing of consideration and readiness and willingness of the 

<<PAGE 17>>
 
17
plaintiff and breach by the defendant. A decree for specific 
performance merely declares the right of the decree-holder to 
have a deed of transfer executed in his favour in respect of the 
property covered by the decree. The decree itself does not 
transfer title. Title passes only upon execution and registration 
of a conveyance in accordance with the Transfer of Property 
Act and the Registration Act.  
Since the agreement for sale dated 23.02.1998 has been 
validly proved and passing of consideration has been 
established by consistent and credible evidence there exists no 
legal impediment to granting decree. The Courts below upon 
proper appreciation of evidence and correct application of law 
committed no illegality or material irregularity in decreeing 
the suit. The decisions cited by the petitioner being 
distinguishable on facts are not applicable.  
Accordingly the Rule having no merit is discharged. The 
judgments and decrees of the Courts below are hereby 
affirmed.  
Communicate this judgment to the concerned Court and 
send down the lower Courts’ record.

input_summary: In July 2000, the first OPPOSITE PARTY sued PETITIONER for specific performance of a 23.02.1998 sale agreement priced at Tk. 1,20,000, alleging Tk. 75,000 earnest-money payment, tender of the remaining Tk. 45,000 within four months of the six-month term, admission in local arbitration, and non-execution in July 2000. Contesting in September 2001, PETITIONER claimed joint ownership, denied any contract, payment, or arbitration, alleged his signature was copied from a September 1996 gift deed for the plaintiff's mother, and cited a September 2000 forgery case. After concurrent decrees for the plaintiff in August 2004 and June 2013, PETITIONER sought revision under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure alleging shifted burden of proof, unilateral unregistered contract, joint-title dispute, and unsafe signature comparison without experts; OPPOSITE PARTIES invoked Sections 101-103 of the Evidence Act.
explanation: Applying Sections 45, 47, 61-65, 67, 73, 101, and 103 of the Evidence Act 1872 alongside Order 11 Rule 14 and Order 16 Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the Court held the plaintiff discharged his Section 101 burden through consistent testimony from attesting witnesses and the scribe plus stamp purchase in PETITIONER's name, shifting the Section 103 forgery onus onto PETITIONER, who never produced or summoned the 03.09.1996 gift deed. Advisory expert opinion under Section 45 was unnecessary where Section 73 comparison with admitted court signatures confirmed authorship.

<<PAGE 1>>
Bench: 
Mr. Justice Md. Ali Reza 
 
Civil Revision No. 2856 of 2023 
 
Md. Emdadul Haque (Foring) and others 
         ......petitioners  
                              -Versus- 
Mst. Reful Bibi and others 
                                              ......opposite parties  
       
Mr. ABM Makdum Hossain Dewan with 
Mr. Md. Enamul Haq, Advocates  
 
 
               ......for the petitioners  
 
Mr. Mr. Shah Newaz, Advocate 
 
 
 
 
......for the opposite parties 
 
Heard on: 05.01.2026, 08.01.2026 and 
21.01.2026 
 
Judgment on: 22.01.2026 
 
 
 
In the instant revision Rule was issued on 05.06.2023 
calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the 
judgment and decree dated 15.03.2023 passed by the 
Additional District Judge, Chapainawabgonj in Civil Appeal 
No. 123 of 2013 thereby reversing the judgment and decree 
dated 17.06.2013 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, 
Gomastapur Court, Chapainawabgonj in Other Class Suit No. 
87 of 2005  should not be set aside and/or such other of further 
order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and 
proper.  

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
The opposite parties as plaintiff filed Other Class Suit 
No. 87 of 2005 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Gomastapur, 
Chapai Nawabgonj for declaration of title and partition and the 
suit was filed on 30.07.2005.  
The case of the plaintiffs in short is that Moksed 
Mondal, Hasim Uddin, Johoruddin, Abdur Rahman were 
owners in possession of the Ka and Kha schedule land in equal 
share of 4 annas. While they were in possession and 
enjoyment of the land they transferred 0.34 acres of land of 
Kha schedule from plot number 78/344. At the time of 
possession and enjoying the land of Ga schedule Hasim Uddin 
left his paternal homestead and went to Babargaon Village and 
started to stay there and conferred the duty to record his name 
in S.A. record upon his brother Moksed Mondal with the firm 
belief that S.A. record would be prepared duly in his name. 
Thereafter Hasim Uddin died leaving behind his one wife 
named Kaju Bibi and one son named Joynal Abedin and two 
daughters named Rabeya Khatun and Hazera Khatun and 
these heirs and successors of Hasim Uddin became owners of 
the land left by Hasim Uddin and used to possess and enjoy 
the same jointly with other co sharers. C.S. recorded tenant 
Abdur Rahman transferred .32 acres of land from plot 126 to 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
one Rozza Khatun who was the wife of Johor Uddin. After 
death of Moksed Mondal his two sons Idris Ali and Solaiman 
and wife Joygunnesa became heirs and successors. Another 
C.S. recorded tenant Abdur Rahman died leaving behind two 
daughters named Ramiza and Monowara and wife Anowara 
and brother Johor Uddin who bacame heirs and successors and 
used to possess and enjoy the land in dispute jointly. The 
plaintiffs have conferred the duty upon Idris Mondol to record 
their names in R.S. record and they had firm belief that R.S. 
record would be recorded in their names properly. In the 
circumstance while maintaining joint possession they asked 
the defendants to make partition of the suit land but were 
refused on 01.04.2005 on the plea that they have no title over 
the suit land as the R.S. record has not been prepared and 
published in their names. On 30.05.2005 after obtaining the 
certified copies of R.S. and S.A. khatians they came to learn 
that R.S. record has not been duly recorded. The father of the 
plaintiffs never transferred his share of the land to Moksed 
Mondol or his heirs. Hence the suit.      
The petitioners as defendants 1-3 and 8-19 contested the 
suit by filing a written statement denying the material 
averments made in the plaint contending inter alia that 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
Moksed Mondol, Hasimuddin, Johuruddin and Abdur Rahman 
were four brothers and recorded tenants as well in C.S. 
khatians 117 and 162 having equal shares of 4 (four) annas 
each as mentioned in schedules Ka and Kha to the plaints. The 
land described in schedule Ka is homestead land and the lands 
described in schedules Kha and Ga are agricultural land. 
Hasimuddin decided to leave his paternal homestead land and 
settled in a nearby Baburghon village and transferred his 4 
(four) annas share of land to Moksed Mondol by registered 
deed number 3498 dated 07.09.1943 and thus Moksed Mondol 
while had been in possession and enjoyment in 8 annas share 
of Kha and Ga schedules land S.A. record 173 was recorded 
and published in his name and after few years when 
Hasimuddin proposed to transfer his share of land from Ka 
schedule Moksed Mondol got the land by registered deed. 
Both the deeds were in the custody of Johuruddin and after his 
death these two deeds came under the custody of his son 
named Abul Hossain who hid the deeds and gave the date of 
the deed in respect of Kha schedule land and the deed in 
respect of Ka schedule land remained hidden. However while 
had been in possession and enjoyment Moksed Mondol died 
leaving behind one wife Joigunnessa and two sons Iddris 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
Ahmed and Solaiman in whose names R.S. khatian 106 was 
recorded in respect of 8 annas share. Joigunnessa died leaving 
behind two sons named Iddris and Solaiman who became heirs 
and successors. Iddris transferred his share of land from Ka 
and Kha schedules to defendants 1-3 and 4-7 by wasiyatnama 
deed number 52 dated 23.06.1997. After death of Solaiman his 
wife defendant 19 and three sons and eight daughters who are 
defendants 8-10 and 11-18 became heirs and successors and 
they have been maintaining title and possession in 8 annas 
share of land. R.S. records 105 and 107 have been duly 
recorded in respect of Ga schedule land with regard to 8 annas 
share. Plaintiffs have got no title and possession in the suit 
land and the suit is liable to be dismissed.  
Trial Court framed as many as five issues as to 
maintainability, defect of party, limitation, whether the 
plaintiff has title and possession in the suit land, whether the 
plaintiff is entitled to have the reliefs as prayed for. During the 
course of trial plaintiffs examined three witnesses and 
defendants examined four witness and both the parties 
adduced documentary evidence in order to prove their 
respective cases. 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
Upon perusal of the records and hearing the parties trial 
Court dismissed the suit by judgment and decree dated 
17.06.2013 on the finding that the suit is barred by limitation 
and the plaintiffs failed prove their title and possession over 
the suit land.  
As against the same plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal 123 
of 2013 before the District Judge, Chapainawabgonj which on 
transfer was heard by the Additional District Judge, 
Chapainawabgonj who was pleased to allow the appeal by 
judgment and decree dated 15.03.2023 and granted saham of 
12 decimals of land to the plaintiff.  
Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment 
passed by the appellate Court the defendants came before this 
Court with this revision and obtained Rule on 05.06.2023.  
Learned Advocate Mr. ABM Makdum Hossain Dewan 
along with Mr. Md. Enamul Haq appearing on behalf of the 
petitioners submits that the appellate Court committed error of 
law resulting in an error in such decree occasioning failure of 
justice in decreeing the suit upon misreading and non-
consideration of material evidence and the impugned 
judgment is not a proper judgment of reversal in that the 
appellate Court failed to follow the provision laid down in 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the 
impugned judgment being perverse and misconceived is liable 
to be set aside. He refers to section 9 of the Partition Act read 
with section 44 of the Transfer of Property Act and submits 
that the appellate Court went against the relevant law and 
wrongly passed the impugned judgment occasioning failure of 
justice. At one stage he contends that this is a fit case for 
remand to the appellate Court under Order 41 Rules 23 and 25 
of the Code of Civil Procedure and also for giving opportunity 
to the petitioners for production of additional evidence in the 
appellate Court under Order 41 Rule 27 of the Code of Civil 
Procedure in the interest of justice in default whereof the 
cause of justice would stand frustrated. In support of his 
submission he refers to the case of Mohabbat Vs. Asadullah 
Khan and others reported in PLD 1989 SC 112.   
Learned Advocate Mr. Shah Newaz appearing on behalf 
of the opposite parties submits that the trial Court committed 
error of law resulting in an error in such decree occasioning 
failure of justice in dismissing the suit upon fanciful 
consideration. He submits that the Senior Assistant Judge 
failed to consider that S.A. record has been prepared correctly 
in the name of the predecessor of the plaintiffs and the 

<<PAGE 8>>
 
8
defendants also failed to produce any deed showing execution 
by Hasimuddin in favour of Moksed Ali in respect of land of 
C.S. khatian 117 described in schedule Ka to the plaint and as 
such since there is no basis of R.S. khatian prepared in the 
name of the defendants in respect of the land of schedule Ka 
the appellate Court upon proper consideration of evidence 
correctly decreed the suit.  
He also submits that the trial Court committed error of 
law occasioning failure of justice in holding that the suit is 
barred by limitation but failed to appreciate that against a 
wrong record of right the person whose interest is affected is 
required to file the suit seeking declaration of title within six 
years from the date the person in whose name record has been 
wrongly prepared and finally published raises claim on the 
basis of wrong record or in other words the cause of action 
arises from the date of denial and in support of his submission 
he referred to the case of Bangladesh Vs. A.K.M Abdul Hye, 
reported in 56 DLR(AD) 53. He prays that the rule be 
discharged.      
Heard the learned Advocates of both sides and perused 
the materials on record.    

<<PAGE 9>>
 
9
 
Plaintiffs filed the suit for declaration of title and 
partition in respect of C.S. records 117 and 162 and claim 12 
acres of land in 4 annas share from C.S. record 117 and 2.091
2  
acres of land in 4 annas share from C.S. record 162 as 
mentioned in schedules Ka and Ga respectively. It is admitted 
that Moksed, Hasimuddin, Johuruddin and Rahman were four 
brothers and tenants as well in those records in 4 annas share 
each. Plaintiffs claim that the R.S. record 106 corresponding 
to C.S. record 117 is correctly prepared in the names of the 
plaintiffs but R.S. records 105, 201, 207 corresponding to C.S. 
record 162 are wrong being recorded in the names of the 
defendants.  
 
Defendants claim that Hasimuddin transferred his entire 
share of C.S. records 117 and 162 to the predecessor of 
defendants. In its support defendants produced the xerox copy 
of the kabala number 3498 dated 07.09.1943 with a notorial 
certificate dated 12.07.2007 authenticated by P.K. Agarwala 
through registration number 45 of 1999 from Malda, West 
Bengal along with an envelop bearing seal of India Postage 
dated 29.07.2007 which is marked in evidence as Exhibit-D 
and D.W. 4 was examined in this respect and accordingly R.S. 

<<PAGE 10>>
 
10
records 105, 107 were prepared in the names of the defendants 
as apparent from Exhibit-C series. Plaintiffs claim that the said 
deed has no evidentiary value as it was not authenticated by 
the High Commission. However upon consideration of the 
facts and circumstances of the case and the entire evidence on 
record it clearly transpires that the predecessor of plaintiffs 
had executed such deed in favour of the predecessor of 
defendants. The trial Court and the appellate Court 
concurrently found as a fact that the said deed is genuine and 
plaintiffs failed to place before this Court any grievance 
showing convincing and reliable evidence to prove that 
transfer by Exhibit-D is not genuine. Therefore it appears that 
the said deed was duly executed and by virtue of and in 
consequence of exhibit-D the subsequent R.S. records Exhibit-
C series were prepared in the names of the defendants 
whereby the title of the plaintiffs as recorded in C.S. khatian 
162 stood extinguished. Since R.S. khatians Exhibit-3 series 
have their basis the said khatians carry a strong presumptive 
value under section 144A of the State Acquisition and 
Tenancy Act and such presumption shall prevail until it is 
proved otherwise.  

<<PAGE 11>>
 
11
 
Defendants have not filed the document showing their 
acquisition of title from Hasimuddin in favour of Moksed in 
respect of the land of C.S. khatian 117. The predecessor of 
plaintiffs named Hasimuddin had interest in 4 annas share 
equivalent to 0.12 acres of land out of 0.48 acres in C.S. 
khatian 117. Defendants claim that the said deed was in the 
custody of Johiruddin and upon his death it came into 
possession of his son Abul Hossain who concealed the said 
deed and as he did not disclose the date and number of the 
deed the defendants could not produce the same before the 
Court. Defendants failed to take any step to cause production 
of the said deed through the custodian thereof or otherwise 
and did not invoke the provision of law relating to summoning 
and production of documents under Order 11 Rule 14 or Order 
16 Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure nor took any other 
necessary legal measure for bringing the said deed before the 
Court. It appears that the S.A. khatian 122 Exhibit-2 was duly 
prepared and finally published in the names of the plaintiffs in 
accordance with their corresponding shares under C.S. khatian 
117 but the R.S. khatian 106 Exhibit-3 corresponding to 
Exhibit-2 was wrongly prepared in the names of the 
defendants. So the claim of the defendants that Hasimuddin 

<<PAGE 12>>
 
12
sold the land of the said C.S. khatian to Moksed is not proved. 
Accordingly it appears that out of 0.48 acres of land under 
R.S. khatian 106 the plaintiffs have title to 0.12 acres being 4 
annas share corresponding to C.S. khatian 117.  
 
  The submissions made by learned Advocate Mr. Dewan 
by invoking Section 9 of the Partition Act and Section 44 of 
the Transfer of Property Act are completely irrelevant to the 
fact and law involved in the present case. Moreover the prayer 
for remand sought for the purpose of substantiating the 
defendants’ documents is untenable since the said documents 
could not be located as admitted by the defendants themselves. 
Hence the prayer for remand is entirely misconceived and it is 
the settled principle of law that remand cannot be granted as a 
matter of course at the instance of any party. In the absence of 
any legal foundation the submissions made by Mr. Dewan are 
hereby overridden and the ratio as given in the case referred to 
by him is not at all applicable in the present case.  
 
In view of the observations made above the plaintiffs 
having title shall get separate allotment of 0.12 acres of land 
as claimed in schedule-Ka and the same shall be executed in 
terms of the ordering portion of the judgment passed by the 
appellate Court.  

<<PAGE 13>>
 
13
 
Since the judgment passed by the appellate Court is 
correct and lawful the same is hereby affirmed and 
accordingly this Rule having no merit is liable to be 
discharged. The judgment and decree passed by the trial Court 
is set aside.  
 
Consequently the Rule is discharged.  
The order of stay passed by this Court stands vacated.  
Communicate this judgment to the concerned Court and 
send down the lower Courts’ record.  
 
 
Md. Ali Reza, J:

input_summary: In July 2005, OPPOSITE PARTIES sued to partition homestead Schedule Ka and agricultural Schedules Kha and Ga held in equal four-anna shares by four brothers: PERSON_1, plaintiffs' predecessor PERSON_2, PERSON_3, and PERSON_4. OPPOSITE PARTIES alleged relocated PERSON_2 and his heirs entrusted SA and RS recording to PERSON_1 and PERSON_1's son PERSON_5 while maintaining joint possession until April 2005. Contesting PETITIONERS, claiming under PERSON_1's sons PERSON_5 (via a June 1997 wasiyatnama) and PERSON_6, pleaded PERSON_2 sold his agricultural share by a September 1943 deed and his Schedule Ka share by a deed concealed by PERSON_3's son PERSON_7. After a 2013 non-suit was reversed in March 2023 to allot OPPOSITE PARTIES 12 decimals in Schedule Ka, PETITIONERS sought revision citing Order 41 Rules 23, 25, 27, and 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure, Section 9 Partition Act, and Section 44 Transfer of Property Act.
explanation: While concurrent findings on the genuine 07.09.1943 sale deed gave defendants' agricultural RS khatians presumptive force under Section 144A of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, defendants produced no deed from plaintiffs' predecessor covering the 0.48-acre Schedule Ka homestead and took no steps under Order 11 Rule 14 or Order 16 Rule 6 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 to summon the allegedly concealed instrument, leaving plaintiffs' SA-backed four-anna title to 0.12 acres intact. Partition Act and Transfer of Property Act pleas were irrelevant, and remand could not be ordered for an unlocated deed.

In the instant revision Rule was issued on 21.11.2022 
calling upon the opposite parties 1-11 to show cause as to why 
the judgment and decree dated 04.10.2022 passed by the 
Additional District Judge, Gopalgonj in Title Appeal No. 51 of 
2021 disallowing the appeal thereby affirming the judgment 
and decree dated 28.03.2021 passed by the Assistant Judge, 
Kotalipara, Gopalgonj in Title Suit No. 21 of 2014 should not 
be set aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed 
as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
The present opposite party 1 as plaintiff instituted Title 
Suit No. 21 of 2014 on 20.03.2014 in the Court of the 
Assistant Judge, Kotalipara, Gopalganj seeking a declaration 
that the appointment of defendant 4 to the post of Peon-cum-
Guard in No. 49 Uttarpara Madrasha Songlogno Government 
Primary School, Kotalipara, Gopalganj pursuant to the 
impugned office order dated 10.03.2014 is illegal, void, 
without lawful authority and not binding upon the plaintiff.  
It is stated in the plaint that a notice was published for 
appointment to the said post. The plaintiff participated in the 
interview held on 08.02.2014 and secured first position 
therein. Subsequently defendant 3 allegedly instructed the 
managing committee of the said school to appoint defendant 4 
who is the present petitioner to the advertised post and 
accordingly an office order dated 10.03.2014 was issued 
appointing him.  
The plaintiff asserts that having secured first position in 
the interview he is legally entitled to be appointed to the said 
post. The appointment of defendant 4 and the recommendation 
made by defendant 3 are alleged to be baseless, illegal and in 
violation of the Recruitment Policy for Appointment of 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
Manpower through Outsourcing (BEV−p¡¢pw Hl j¡dÉ−j plL¡¢l

Defendant Numbers 1, 2 and 4 contested the suit by 
filing separate written statements denying all material 
allegations made in the plaint.  
The specific case of defendant 1 is that the plaintiff did 
participate in the interview held on 08.02.2014 and stood first 
therein. However defendant 4 who is the present petitioner in 
this civil revision allegedly secured 3rd position in the merit 
list and therefore his appointment to the advertised post is 
illegal.  
On the other hand the specific case of defendant 4 is that 
after completion of the viva voce examination the scrutiny and 
recruitment committee of the said school prepared a panel 
based on the overall assessment including the physical fitness 
of the candidates. It is stated that the present petitioner is 
S.S.C. passed and physically fit whereas the plaintiff was 
physically weak and unsuitable for the post. According to 
defendant 4 although the petitioner was placed at serial 3 in 
the list and the plaintiff at serial 1 but the list was duly 
forwarded to the UNO for approval in accordance with law.  

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
It is the further case of the petitioner that he was 
physically fit, competent and duly qualified for the post in 
question. It is stated that after consultation with the local 
Chairman and the representative deputed by the local Member 
of Parliament he was appointed to the advertised post of Peon-
cum-Guard. Pursuant thereto he joined the said post upon 
complying with all procedural requirements and relevant rules. 
Hence the suit is liable to be dismissed.  
The trial Court framed as many as five issues for 
determination. During trial the plaintiff examined himself as 
P.W. 1 and adduced Exhibit-1 as documentary evidence. 
Defendant 4 examined himself as D.W. 1. The defendant 
adduced documentary evidence marked as Exhibits-Ka(1) and 
Ka(2) in support of his case.  
Upon consideration of the pleadings of the parties along 
with the oral and documentary evidence on record and the 
relevant laws the trial Court by judgment and decree dated 
28.03.2021 decreed the suit.   
Being aggrieved thereby the defendant number 4 
preferred Title Appeal No. 51 of 2021 before the District 
Judge, Gopalganj. The appeal was subsequently transferred to 
the Court of the Additional District Judge who by judgment 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
and decree dated 04.10.2022 dismissed the appeal affirming 
the judgment and decree of the trial Court.  
Being further aggrieved the defendant number 4 filed the 
present civil revision before this Court and obtained Rule on 
21.11.2022.  
Learned Advocate Mr. Md. Masud Hasan Chowdhury 
along with Mr. M. Ashraf Ali appearing on behalf of the 
petitioner submits that both the Courts below failed to follow 
the provisions of the Recruitment Policy for Appointment of 
Peon-cum-Guard in Government Primary Schools through 
Outsourcing, 2012 (BEV−p¡¢pw Hl j¡dÉ−j plL¡¢l fË¡b¢jL ¢hcÉ¡m−ul 
cçl£ L¡j fËql£ ¢e−u¡N e£¢aj¡m¡, 2012) [hereinafter referred to as the 
nitimala] and thereby wrongly passed the impugned judgment 
and decree committing error of law resulting in such decree 
occasioning failure of justice.  
He further submits that under the said nitimala the 
Selection Committee is required to prepare a panel of three 
candidates against each post and the appointing authority is 
empowered to appoint any one candidate from the said panel. 
Referring to the nitimala he contends that nowhere therein is it 
provided that the candidate placed at serial 1 in the merit list 
must mandatorily be appointed to the advertised post.    

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
According to him since the petitioner was included in the 
panel of three candidates duly prepared by the Selection 
Committee the competent authority lawfully appointed him. 
The Courts below failed to consider this vital legal aspect and 
thereby committed error of law occasioning failure of justice. 
He further contends that the petitioner was appointed to the 
post of Peon-cum-Guard strictly in compliance with the 
procedure prescribed by the statute and the nitimala and he 
joined the post accordingly. If any irregularity occurred the 
same was attributable to the authority concerned and not to the 
petitioner. The Courts below without considering the 
petitioner’s lawful right arising from his inclusion in the panel 
erroneously decreed the suit thereby committing error of law 
occasioning failure of justice which cannot be sustained in 
law.  
He next submits that although the plaintiff did not pray 
for any consequential relief both the Courts below in clear 
violation of law granted a decree effectively reinstating the 
plaintiff in service. Referring to Section 42 of the Specific 
Relief Act he submits that a mere declaration cannot be 
granted where the plaintiff being able to seek further relief 
omits to do so. In the absence of a prayer for consequential 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
relief or mandatory injunction the decree as passed is legally 
unsustainable and liable to be set aside. He further points out 
that the petitioner himself did not commit any illegality in the 
matter of his appointment and he cannot be penalized for any 
alleged procedural lapse on the part of the authority. The 
Courts below failed to consider this material aspect and thus 
committed error of law in passing the impugned decree 
occasioning failure of justice and since the Rule has merit the 
same may be made absolute. In support of his submission he 
refers to the cases of Dhunat Degree College Vs. Md. Abdus 
Samad, 49 DLR 38; TCB Vs. Syed Sajeduzzaman, 40 DLR 
406; Jahir Uddin Vs. Rupali Bank, 12 BLC(AD) 114; Rupali 
Bank Vs. Md. Arab Ali, 7 BLC(AD) 1; Dhaka WASA Vs. 
Matiar Rahman, 7 BLC(AD) 4; Habibur Rahman Vs. DC 
Patuakhali, 51 DLR 70.   
On the other hand learned Advocate Ms. Afifa Begum 
along with Mr. Md. Abdur Razzak appearing on behalf of the 
plaintiff-opposite party submits that the nitimala was 
promulgated on 27.09.2012 and was subsequently amended on 
several occasions. She submits that by amendment dated 
26.01.2015 Niti 7(2) conferred absolute power upon the local

8
among the three selected candidates. The said amended

She further submits that from the nitimala of 2012 upto 
the amended versions including the nitimala of 2019 the 
provision relating to allocation of 20 marks for viva-voce 
examination has never been repealed which clearly manifests 
the legislative intent that candidates securing the highest 
marks out of the allotted 20 marks in viva-voce would receive 
priority in appointment. Such intent is also reflected in Niti 
7(Kha) of the nitimala, 2019. He submits that Clause 7 of the 
nitimala dated 09.12.2012 clearly provides that defendant 3 
had no authority to appoint any candidate but only to approve 
the panel of three candidates and thereafter defendants 1 and 2 
were competent to appoint in compliance with Clause 7(5) of 
the nitimala, 2012. According to her both the Courts below 
upon proper appreciation of the pleadings and evidence and 
the applicable nitimala lawfully decreed the suit. The 
concurrent findings of fact and law do not call for interference 
in revision under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil 
Procedure.  

<<PAGE 9>>
 
9
She lastly submits that if the plaintiff is otherwise 
entitled to any relief for substantial justice the Court is 
empowered to grant appropriate relief in accordance with law. 
Since the impugned judgments have ensured justice in the 
facts and circumstances of the case the same may be 
maintained and the Rule be discharged. Supporting her 
submission she refers to the cases of DCC Vs. Shamsur 
Rahman, 59 DLR 207; General Manager, Rangpur Palli 
Bidyut Samity Vs. Md. Ali Reza, 11 MLR(AD) 382; 
Bangladesh Railway Vs. Din Mohammad, 7 BLT(AD) 361; 
Jibon Bima Vs. Mustafa Hussain, 50 DLR 411.  
Heard the learned Advocates and perused the materials 
on record and the laws relating thereto.   
It is admitted by both parties that in the recruitment 
process for the post of Peon-cum-Guard of No. 49, Uttarpara 
Madrasha Songlogno Government Primary School the 
plaintiff secured first position and defendant 4 secured third 
position in the viva-voce examination.  
The case of the plaintiff is that the appointing approving 
authority namely defendant 3 illegally and without lawful 
basis approved the appointment of defendant 4 bypassing the 
plaintiff who stood first in the merit list. On the other hand 

<<PAGE 10>>
 
10
defendant 4 contends that among the three shortlisted 
candidates he was physically stronger and more suitable and 
therefore his appointment was duly approved by the 
appointing approving authority.  
Under Clause 2(g) of the Recruitment Policy of 
Appointment of Peon-cum-Guard in Government Primary 
Schools through Outsourcing, 2012 (hereinafter referred to as 
the nitimala) the Upazila Nirbahi Officer of the concerned 
Upazila is defined as the “appointing approving authority.” In 
the present case defendant 3 is the said appointing approving 
authority.  
P.W. 1 stated in cross-examination that a viva-voce 
examination was held and he secured first position therein. 
D.W. 1 stated that one of the conditions of appointment was 
physical fitness. However he admitted in cross-examination 
that he did not submit any document proving that he was 
physically more fit than the plaintiff. He further admitted that 
no document was produced showing that the plaintiff was 
physically unfit. From the appointment memorandum dated 
22.03.2014 issued by the Headmaster’s office it appears that 
the appointment of defendant 4 was purportedly made 
pursuant to the nitimala published on 09.12.2012 and the 

<<PAGE 11>>
 
11
amendment dated 07.10.2013 and such appointment was based 
upon the result of the viva-voce examination subject to 
approval. Clause 7(2) of the nitimala 2012 provides that the 
Selection and Recruitment Committee shall conduct a viva-
voce examination carrying 20 marks and upon assessment of 
physical fitness prepare a panel of three qualified candidates 
and forward the same to the appointing approving authority.  
Clause 7(3) provides that within 30 days of receipt of 
such recommendation the appointing approving authority shall 
in consultation with the Upazila Parishad Chairman and the 
concerned Member of Parliament accord approval or if 
approval is withheld then record the reasons and issue 
necessary direction.  
Clause 7(5) provides that upon approval and in absence 
of contrary direction the candidate placed at serial 1 of the 
panel shall be offered appointment subject to the prescribed 
monthly service charge and terms of contract.  
Clause 7(8) further provides that if the approved 
candidate fails to join within the stipulated time the candidate 
placed at serial 2 and in his absence the candidate placed at 
serial 3 shall be offered appointment. The 2013 amendment 
modified Clause 7(5) by allowing at least one week’s time for 

<<PAGE 12>>
 
12
joining from the date of issuance of appointment letter and 
provided that if the appointee fails to join within the period or 
resigns within six months the next candidate in order shall be 
appointed. Upon conjoint reading of Clauses 7(2), 7(3), 7(5) 
and 7(8) of the original and amended nitimala it is evident that 
although a panel of three candidates is to be prepared the 
statutory scheme clearly attaches primacy to the candidate 
placed at serial 1 in the merit list. Departure from such order is 
permissible only in accordance with the structured mechanism 
provided therein.  
In the present case the memorandum dated 10.03.2014 
issued from the office of defendant 3 does not disclose any re-
fixation or lawful rearrangement of the order of merit. There is 
no material on record showing that the order of preference was 
reconsidered upon consultation with the Upazila Parishad 
Chairman and the concerned Member of Parliament. There is 
no explanation as to why the candidates placed at serial 
numbers 1 and 2 were bypassed and the candidate placed at 
serial 3 was approved. From the records produced pursuant to 
the Court’s requisition it appears that in the viva-voce 
examination the plaintiff secured 18 marks out of 20 and stood 

<<PAGE 13>>
 
13
first and Ibrahim Molla secured 15.67 marks and stood second 
and defendant 4 secured 15 marks and stood third.   
The very purpose of preparing a merit list is to ensure 
appointment of the most meritorious candidate. If the 
appointing approving authority is permitted to ignore the order 
of merit without recorded justification it would open the door 
to arbitrariness and frustrate the objective of the nitimala.  
Since no documentary evidence has been produced to 
substantiate the claim that defendant 4 was physically superior 
or that the plaintiff was physically unfit the plea of physical 
superiority remains unproved. Therefore this Court finds that 
the appointing approving authority acted in violation of 
Clauses 7(3) and 7(5) of the nitimala, 2012 in approving the 
appointment of defendant 4. The procedure prescribed by law 
was not followed and the approval was granted without lawful 
basis.  
It is true that the plaintiff instituted the present suit 
primarily challenging the memorandum dated 10.03.2014 and 
sought declaratory relief. However under Order 7 Rule 7 of 
the Code of Civil Procedure the Court is empowered to grant 
appropriate relief consistent with the pleadings and supported 
by evidence even if such relief has not been expressly prayed 

<<PAGE 14>>
 
14
for provided that the foundation for such relief exists in the 
plaint and evidence. In the present case the entire cause of 
action revolves around wrongful denial of appointment to the 
plaintiff despite his entitlement under the nitimala. The 
consequential relief of appointment flows directly and 
inevitably from the declaration sought. Law does not hesitate 
to grant substantive relief when the materials on record justify 
such course and when denial thereof would perpetuate 
illegality.  For securing ends of justice and to give meaningful 
effect to the statutory framework the Courts below rightly 
granted effective relief in favour of the plaintiff. The ratio of 
the case laws referred to by the plaintiff-opposite party is 
consistent with the facts and circumstances of the present case.   
Since the appointing approving authority violated the 
mandatory provisions of the nitimala, 2012 in approving the 
appointment of defendant 4 bypassing the first candidate in the 
merit list without lawful justification the approval dated 
10.03.2014 is illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiff.  
Accordingly the appointment of defendant 4 pursuant to 
memorandum dated 10.03.2014 is declared illegal and 
cancelled. The said appointment shall not be binding upon the 
plaintiff. The concerned authority is directed to appoint the 

<<PAGE 15>>
 
15
plaintiff to the post in question within 30 days from the date of 
receipt of this judgment in accordance with the nitimala, 2012. 
The plaintiff shall stand substituted in the said post within the 
stipulated period. Any civil or criminal liability if arising from 
acts committed by defendant 4 during his tenure shall not 
attach to the plaintiff.  
The decisions cited by the learned Advocate for the 
petitioner having been rendered on facts and circumstances 
materially distinguishable from those of the present case are 
not applicable herein. Since both the Courts below correctly 
appreciated the evidence and law and committed no 
jurisdictional error or illegality or material irregularity 
occasioning failure of justice within the meaning of section 
115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure this Court finds no 
merit in the rule.  
Accordingly the Rule is discharged.  
The judgments and decrees of the Courts below are 
hereby affirmed.  
Since the relief of appointment granted in favour of the 
plaintiff is in the nature of consequential relief flowing from 
the declaration sought and since such relief attracts payment of 
ad velorem court fee under the Court Fees Act the plaintiff is 

<<PAGE 16>>
 
16
directed to pay the highest ad velorem court fee as prescribed 
under the present law on the valuation of the consequential 
relief within 30 working days from the date of receipt of this 
judgment. In default of payment of such court fee within the 
time stipulated above the decree insofar as it relates to the 
consequential relief of appointment shall stand recalled 
automatically without further reference to the Court and the 
decree shall remain confined only to the declaratory relief as 
sought for. Office is directed to verify compliance before 
issuance of the decree.  
No order as to costs.  
The order of stay passed by this Court stands vacated.  
Communicate this judgment to the concerned Court and 
send down the lower Courts’ record.  
 
 
Md. Ali Reza, J: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Naher-B.O

Bench:
