In the instant revision Rule was issued calling upon the 
opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned 
judgment and decree dated 11.03.2025 passed by the learned 
Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Jashore in Title Appeal 
Number 21 of 2024 allowing the appeal thereby reversing the 
judgment and decree dated 13.02.2024 passed by the learned 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
Senior Assistant Judge, Jashore Sadar, Jashore in Title Suit 
Number 127 of 2023 should not be set aside and/or such other 
or further order or orders be passed as to this Court may seem 
fit and proper.  
The petitioners as plaintiff instituted Title Suit 81 of 
2002 on 16.09.2002 in the Court of the Assistant Judge at 
Keshabpur, Jashore seeking a declaration that the Khas 
khatian prepared in the name of defendant 1 and the eviction 
notices dated 03.08.2002 and 07.09.2002 issued by defendants 
2 and 3 are illegal, incorrect and not binding upon the 
plaintiffs. Subsequently the suit was renumbered on 
09.03.2023 as Title Suit 127 of 2023.  
The concise facts of the plaint are that 35 decimals of 
land out of former C.S. plot 271 were settled by the heirs of 
C.S. tenant in favour of Ibrahim Biswas by virtue of patta deed 
2034 dated 03.05.1944 and he entered into possession thereof. 
While possessing 27 decimals being 12 annas share out of the 
said 35 decimals as owner in possession Ibrahim Biswas died 
leaving behind three sons namely Gohar Ali, Ahar Ali and 
Baker Ali as his heirs. Subsequently Gohar Ali died leaving 
behind one son Rezaul Haque. In 1959 when the then 
Tahsildar attempted to dispossess the heirs of Ibrahim Biswas 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
from the said land they filed an objection before the then Joint 
Collector. Upon hearing the matter the Joint Collector by 
order dated 11.12.1959 held that the land of the suit plot being 
vacant non-agricultural land was not liable to acquisition. 
Consequently the acquisition proceeding in respect of the suit 
land was dropped and the said land was released during the 
preparation of the acquisition roll relating to the concerned 
cattle market. However in 1961 when the local Tahsildar again 
proposed to auction the suit land the predecessors of the 
plaintiffs once again filed an objection before the Joint 
Collector. Upon consideration of the opinion of the 
Government Pleader and other relevant documents the Joint 
Collector by order dated 12.04.1961 directed to stop further 
proceedings observing that the cattle market standing on the 
suit land had already been released. Neverthless on 05.12.1962 
when the local Tahsildar again attempted to dispossess the 
predecessors of the plaintiffs they instituted Title Suit 473 of 
1962 in the 2nd Court of Munsif at Jessore on 08.12.1962 
seeking declaration of their title with confirmation of 
possession and permanent injunction in respect of the suit 
land. In that suit the Government contested by filing written 
statement. The suit was dismissed on 19.06.1965. Thereafter 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
the predecessors of the plaintiffs preferred Title Appeal 180 of 
1965 and the appellate Court by judgment and decree dated 
05.08.1966 allowed the appeal. Subsequently the predecessors 
of the plaintiffs constructed residential houses upon the suit 
land and started residing there with their families. They also 
erected shop rooms and inducted tenants therein by collecting 
rent from them while carrying on their own business 
therefrom. Through two mutation cases during the years 1987-
1988 the land was mutated in their names and separate 
khatians were opened in their favour pursuant to which they 
paid rent separately.  
Later pursuant to the opinion given by the Government 
of Bangladesh following the order dated 08.01.1996 passed in 
Miscellaneous Case 5/XIII/1994-95 the suit land was again 
released in favour of the predecessors of the plaintiffs who 
continued in possession thereof. While in possession Ahar Ali 
and Baker Ali sold a portion of the suit land to plaintiff 1 
Abdul Aziz by virtue of registered sale deed number 5886 
dated 01.12.1991. Subsequently Ahar Ali died leaving behind 
plaintiffs 23-29 and Baker Ali died leaving behind plaintiffs 
30-34 and Rezaul Haque died leaving behind plaintiffs 17-22 
as their heirs. Thus plaintiffs 1 and 17-34 by purchase and 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
inheritance became owners in possession of the suit land and 
continued residing therein in their dwelling houses and 
conducting business in the shop rooms and realizing rent from 
tenants while paying rent to the Government and have been 
possessing the land for more than 70 years. In such 
circumstances the defendants representing the Government 
issued two notices dated 03.08.2002 and 07.09.2002 directing 
the plaintiffs to remove their possession from the suit land or 
to vacate the same.  
According to the plaintiffs the R.S. record prepared in 
the name of the Government under Khas khatian 1 in respect 
of the suit land is erroneous and the said eviction notices are 
illegal. The defendants have no title and possession in the suit 
land. Hence the suit.  
On the other hand defendant 1 contested the suit by 
filing written statement denying the plaintiffs’ case and 
contending inter alia that in C.S. plot 271 under C.S. khatian 
142 there existed 29 decimals of land recorded in the names of 
Budhai Kha and others as temporary lessees. Subsequently 24 
decimals of land under the said plot were recorded in Khas 
khatian 1 in the name of the Government of Bangladesh as 
“Gohata” (cattle market). In the R.S. record the suit land has 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
been recorded in the name of the Government of Bangladesh 
as plots 645 and 646 under Khas khatian 1 as cattle market 
land. After the abolition of the zamindari system all rights, 
interests and possession in such hat-bazar properties vested in 
the Government of Bangladesh and the same was 
subsequently published in the form of a gazette notification in 
1956. Although the predecessors of the plaintiffs were merely 
temporary lessees they instituted Title Suit 473 of 1962 
against the Deputy Commissioner of Jessore claiming 
permanent title. That suit was dismissed on 25.02.1965. 
Thereafter they preferred Title Appeal 180 of 1965 and the 
appellate Court by its judgment dated 15.08.1966 allowed the 
appeal only to the extent of directing that the plaintiffs would 
enjoy twelve-anna subordinate interest until final publication 
of the C.A. Roll.      
The predecessors of the plaintiffs subsequently filed 
Title Suit 839 of 1978 in respect of the same land and lost the 
case. Against that judgment Title Appeal 106 of 1979 was also 
dismissed. Thereafter Civil Revision 806 of 1979 was filed 
before the High Court Division which was discharged on 
contest on 06.12.1983 wherein the High Court held that the 
suit land being hat-bazar property vested in the Government of 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
Bangladesh. A subsequent review petition against the said 
judgment was also dismissed. The plaintiff later obtained 
mutation by misleading the revenue authority through 
Mutation Cases 121/9-1/1987-88 and 122/9-1/1987-88 but 
subsequently the revenue authority by Case Number 
16/XIII/1999-2000 under Section 150 cancelled the earlier 
mutation orders and brought the suit land under Khas khatian 
1 in the name of the Government. After losing further 
miscellaneous proceedings the plaintiffs again filed Appeal 
Case 170 of 1996 before the Divisional Commissioner, 
Khulna which was dismissed upon consideration of the earlier 
litigations. The case filed by the plaintiffs before the Land 
Appeal Board was also dismissed. In accordance with the 
direction given in Title Appeal 180 of 1965 the Government 
following all acquisition formalities published a gazette 
notification dated 21.10.1978 in the C.A. Roll declaring 35 
decimals of land of plot 271 under C.S. khatian 142 as 
Keshabpur cattle market.  
The cattle market situated on the suit land was regularly 
leased out by the Government. However during the 
subsistence of the lease period the Jashore-Satkhira Road was 
constructed across the suit plot which created obstruction in 

<<PAGE 8>>
 
8
operating the cattle market. Later upon widening of the said 
road and due to shortage of space the Government shifted the 
cattle market in 1994 to neighbouring Altapur Mouza. At 
present a daily market is held on suit plot 271 and a regular hat 
sits there on Fridays, Sundays, Tuesdays and Thursdays which 
is leased out by the Government every year. According to the 
defendants the plaintiffs have no title or interest in the suit 
land and have instituted the present suit only to misappropriate 
valuable Government property. The suit being false is liable to 
be dismissed with costs.  
In the suit the trial Court framed as many as twelve 
issues for determination. The plaintiffs examined four 
witnesses while the defendants examined the Union Land 
Assistant Officer as DW 1. Both parties produced 
documentary evidence in support of their respective cases. The 
trial Court also took judicial notice of the Compensation 
Assessment Roll Gazette dated 21.10.1978 and the order dated 
27.02.2000. Subsequently the plaintiffs amended the plaint 
and claimed 18 decimals of land with specific boundaries 
instead of 24 decimals on the ground that 6 decimals had gone 
into the road. Upon hearing the parties and considering the 

<<PAGE 9>>
 
9
evidence on record the trial Court by its judgment and decree 
dated 13.02.2024 decreed the suit.  
Being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree 
defendant 1 the Government of Bangladesh preferred Title 
Appeal 21 of 2024 before the District Judge’s Court at Jessore 
which was subsequently transferred to the Court of the 
Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Jessore. The appellate 
Court by judgment and decree dated 11.03.2025 allowed the 
appeal.  
Being aggrieved thereby the plaintiffs filed the present 
civil revision before this Court and obtained Rule on 
16.04.2025.  
The learned Senior Advocate Mr. Zulfikar Bulbul 
Chowdhury along with learned Advocates Mr. Ahmed 
Nowshed Jamil, Mr. H.M. Borhan and Ms. Sayeda Shoukat 
Ara appearing on behalf of the plaintiff-petitioners submits 
that the appellate Court committed error of law resulting in an 
error in such decree occasioning failure of justice in allowing 
the appeal upon misreading and non-consideration of material 
evidence and also upon misconstruction of the relevant 
documents. He further submits that the findings of the trial 
Court having not been reversed upon assigning proper, cogent 

<<PAGE 10>>
 
10
and lawful reasons the judgment passed by the appellate Court 
cannot be regarded as a proper judgment of reversal within the 
meaning of Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure 
and as such the same being perverse and misconceived is 
liable to be set aside. He further submits that the appellate 
Court failed to consider that the defendants having accepted 
rent from the plaintiffs are estopped from denying the title of 
the plaintiffs and upon misconception of law the appellate 
Court erroneously dismissed the suit thereby occasioning 
miscarriage of justice. He next submits that Exhibit-3 series 
showing mutation in favour of the plaintiffs followed by rent 
receipts marked as Exhibit-4 series are documents evidencing 
possession issued by the competent authority which cannot be 
brushed aside merely upon the assertions of the defendants. 
According to him the trial Court upon proper appreciation of 
the evidence on record rightly decreed the suit but the 
appellate Court without reversing those material findings 
arrived at by the trial Court erroneously dismissed the suit 
which cannot be sustained in accordance with law.  
Referring to Exhibit-8 he very candidly and emphatically 
submits by drawing attention to the operative portion thereof 
that the same clearly indicates that any acquisition by the 

<<PAGE 11>>
 
11
defendants must be made in accordance with law. However 
the allegation advanced by the plaintiffs that the acquisition 
had not been legally effected because the plaintiffs were 
neither served with notice nor awarded compensation in 
accordance with law was not at all considered by the appellate 
Court and as such the appellate Court committed error of law 
occasioning failure of justice in dismissing the suit thereby 
depriving the plaintiffs of their lawful right, title and 
possession in the suit land. He also submits that the defendants 
at one stage contend that the suit land was never released and 
at another stage claim that it had been released and because of 
such contradictory stand taken by the defendants and also due 
to their failure to produce the original volume relating thereto 
before the Court the plaintiffs have been seriously prejudiced. 
The appellate Court without considering these important 
aspects of the matter passed the impugned judgment which has 
resulted in failure of justice. He further submits that it is an 
admitted position that no cattle market presently sits on the 
suit land rather a general market is held there. Moreover 
residential houses and shop rooms belonging to the plaintiffs 
exist on the suit land. He points out that defendants have 
contended that the mutation obtained by the plaintiffs had 

<<PAGE 12>>
 
12
been cancelled through a review case after about twelve years 
and the trial Court found that the said review case was clearly 
barred by limitation. Since the appellate Court did not reverse 
that finding of the trial Court in accordance with law the 
judgment of the appellate Court does not reflect proper 
administration of justice and is liable to be set aside. He 
finally submits that since the Rule involves substantial merit 
the same may be made absolute.  
On the other hand the learned Deputy Attorney General 
Mr. Md. Yousuf Ali along with Mr. Rakib Hossain, Mr. 
Mohammad Salah Uddin Sikder and Ms. Kamrunnahar Lipi, 
learned Assistant Attorneys General appearing on behalf of 
the defendant-Government submits that the appellate Court 
having independently assessed the evidence and reversed the 
judgment passed by the trial Court upon assigning lawful 
reasons committed no error of law resulting in an error in such 
decree occasioning failure of justice and the impugned 
judgment being a proper judgment of reversal in accordance 
with the provisions laid down in Order 41 Rule 31 of the Code 
of Civil Procedure is immune from interference by this Court 
in revision. He strongly submits that since the Compensation 
Assessment Roll has been finally published the suit is barred 

<<PAGE 13>>
 
13
under Section 72 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 
and if the plaintiffs have any grievance they may seek their 
remedy in a suit for compensation. He further submits that the 
finding of the trial Court that the plaintiffs acquired title by 
adverse possession is absolutely perverse and misconceived 
because the plaintiffs never made out such a definite claim in 
their pleadings. The trial Court also failed to appreciate the 
settled principle of law that a claim for declaration of title and 
a claim of title by adverse possession cannot run 
simultaneously since those two claims are mutually 
inconsistent and the latter originates in wrongful possession. 
According to him no evidence has been adduced by the 
plaintiffs to show that their entry into the suit land was hostile 
or that they maintained hostile possession for the statutory 
period. He further submits that since the impugned notices 
were duly issued by the competent authority the judgment 
passed by the appellate Court is perfectly justified. He finally 
submits that the Rule having no merit is liable to be 
discharged. 
Heard the learned Advocates for both sides and perused 
the materials on record and also gone through the impugned 
judgments passed by the courts below. 

<<PAGE 14>>
 
14
This is a suit for declaration of title whereby the 
plaintiffs have sought a declaration that the Khas Khatian 1 
prepared in the name of defendant 1 and the two eviction 
notices dated 03.08.2002 and 07.09.2002 issued by defendants 
2 and 3 are illegal, unlawful, without lawful authority, 
erroneous and without any legal basis. 
The plaintiffs principally claim that the suit land was 
originally acquired by their predecessor Ibrahim Biswas by 
virtue of a patta dated 03.05.1944 which has been marked as 
Exhibit-6. The plaintiffs have produced a certified copy of the 
said deed. It appears from the record that the certified copy 
was obtained on 18.01.1984 which is long before the 
institution of the present suit. Subsequently when the 
defendants threatened to dispossess the plaintiffs from the suit 
land the plaintiffs earlier instituted Title Suit 473 of 1962 on 
08.12.1962 seeking declaration of title with confirmation of 
possession and permanent injunction. 
From paragraphs 3 and 4 of the plaint of that suit which 
has been marked as Exhibit-7 it appears that after the 
provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act came into 
force the defendants on several occasions attempted to take 
khas possession of the disputed hat (cattle market) property 

<<PAGE 15>>
 
15
but due to objections raised by the plaintiffs such attempts 
failed in accordance with law. 
It further appears that in 1959 the local tahsildar once 
issued a notice for eviction whereupon the plaintiffs filed an 
objection before the then Joint Collector who by order dated 
11.12.1959 decided the matter in favour of the plaintiffs. As a 
consequence the acquisition proceedings relating to the 
disputed property were halted and the cattle market concerned 
was released from the acquisition roll. However as further 
proceedings were subsequently initiated and those proceedings 
went against the plaintiffs they instituted Title Suit 473 of 
1962. The trial Court dismissed the suit by judgment dated 
19.06.1965. As against the same the plaintiffs preferred Title 
Appeal 180 of 1965 and the judgment of that appeal has been 
marked as Exhibit-8. 
From 
Exhibit-8 
it 
appears 
that 
although 
the 
Compensation Assessment Roll of the concerned area had 
admittedly been published in the Dhaka Gazette on 
20.03.1962 the appellate Court observed that such publication 
by itself did not confer upon defendant 1 the right to take over 
possession of the cattle market until the compensation 
assessment roll was finally published in accordance with the 

<<PAGE 16>>
 
16
provisions laid down under Sections 42 and 44 of the State 
Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The Gazette notification 
marked as Exhibit-Eno reveals that under the provisions of 
Section 43 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 the 
President declared that the Compensation Assessment Roll 
had been finally published under Section 42 of the said Act in 
respect of the “Sairat Mahal” known as “Keshabpur Cattle 
Market.” In the schedule appended to the said Gazette the 
names of the predecessors of the present plaintiffs of village 
Madhyakul have been mentioned as owners. 
It further appears that the final publication of the 
Compensation Assessment Roll relating to plot 271 
appertaining to C.S. Khatian 142 measuring an area of 35 
decimals of land took place during the period from 27.01.1962 
to 03.03.1962. The said Gazette notification was subsequently 
published in the Bangladesh Gazette Part-I on 26.10.1978 by 
the Ministry of Land Administration and Land Reforms. 
Section 42 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 
(hereinafter called as the Act) deals with the final publication 
of the compensation assessment roll. Once such roll is 
published in the official Gazette it constitutes conclusive 
evidence 
that 
the 
procedures 
for 
determination 
of 

<<PAGE 17>>
 
17
compensation have been duly followed. Section 43 of the Act 
provides for the declaration of such publications. Once such 
declaration is made by the Government the acquisition process 
stands legally concluded. Since the names of the predecessors 
of the plaintiffs are specifically mentioned in the Gazette 
notification of 1978 they are deemed in law to have had 
constructive notice of the acquisition proceedings. Once the 
compensation assessment roll is finalized and published under 
Section 42 it becomes a public record. The plaintiffs’ assertion 
that the roll was not legally completed appears to be a mere 
bald allegation which cannot override the documentary 
evidence contained in the official Gazette. Moreover Section 
114(e) of the Evidence Act provides that the Court may 
presume that official acts have been regularly performed. 
Therefore when the Government produces a Gazette 
notification published under Sections 42 and 43 of the State 
Acquisition and Tenancy Act the law presumes that every 
preliminary step such as survey, valuation, hearing of 
objections and determination of shares was performed in 
accordance with law. 
In such circumstances the burden of proof shifts entirely 
upon the plaintiffs to establish a specific and fundamental 

<<PAGE 18>>
 
18
procedural illegality. A mere allegation that the process was 
not legal is insufficient to unsettle such an old public record. 
Plaintiffs did not show any lawful proof that they approached 
the authority for compensation but were refused. 
Section 43 of the Act acts as the final statutory 
declaration. Once the President or the delegated authority 
declares the publication of the compensation assessment roll 
the acquisition process is legally concluded and the land vests 
in the Government free from all encumbrances and the roll 
becomes a conclusive document evidencing the State’s title. 
The contention of the plaintiffs that the compensation 
assessment roll was not legally completed is therefore clearly 
hit by the statutory bar contained in Section 72 of the State 
Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Furthermore under Section 
114(e) of the Evidence Act this Court is bound to presume the 
regularity of the Gazette notification dated 26.10.1978. Thus a 
suit instituted in 2002 challenging the procedural legality of an 
administrative act completed in 1978 is clearly barred by 
limitation and also by the doctrine of finality of administrative 
actions. The trial Court appears to have proceeded on the 
assumption that since the Government allegedly claimed at 
different times that the land was released and again that it was 

<<PAGE 19>>
 
19
not released the Government was barred by the doctrine of 
estoppel. Such reasoning in the opinion of this Court is legally 
unsustainable. It is a well-settled principle of law that there 
can be no estoppel against a statute. Once the acquisition 
proceedings have been completed in accordance with the 
provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the 
compensation assessment roll has been finally published the 
legal consequence flowing from the statute cannot be defeated 
by invoking the equitable doctrine of estoppel. 
Moreover the alleged order of release dated 08.01.1996 
said to have been passed by the Additional Deputy 
Commissioner (Revenue) cannot override or nullify the legal 
effect of the Gazette notification issued under Sections 42 and 
43 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act because once the 
acquisition is concluded and the property vests in the 
Government no subordinate revenue authority has the 
jurisdiction to release such land in derogation of the statute.  
The trial Court also placed undue emphasis on the 
alleged possession of the plaintiffs and the absence of payment 
of compensation. In this regard it is to be noted that once the 
compensation assessment roll is finally published the statutory 
scheme under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act provides 

<<PAGE 20>>
 
20
a separate remedy for claiming compensation. Any grievance 
relating 
to 
non-payment 
or 
improper 
assessment 
of 
compensation does not invalidate the acquisition itself nor 
does it confer title upon the claimant. Therefore the finding of 
the trial Court that the suit land stood released in favour of the 
plaintiffs and that the Government was barred by the doctrine 
of estoppel is based upon misappreciation of law and 
misreading of the documentary evidence on record particularly 
the Gazette notification marked as Exhibit-Eno. This suit for 
declaration of title cannot be decreed.  
In such circumstances it is apparent that the trial Court 
erroneously arrived at the conclusion that the suit land had 
been released in favour of the plaintiffs whereas the materials 
on record clearly establish that the land had already vested in 
the Government upon final publication of the compensation 
assessment roll. 
In view of the discussions made above and upon 
consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case I find 
no substance in the Rule. 
Accordingly the Rule is discharged. 

<<PAGE 21>>
 
21
The judgment and decree passed by the trial Court are 
hereby set aside and those passed by the appellate Court are 
affirmed. 
The application for addition of party bearing Entry 
Number 6773 dated 19.10.2025 which was earlier ordered to 
be kept with the record on 24.11.25 is taken up for 
consideration at this stage. 
It appears that the applicants claim their interest under 
defendants in respect of the suit property. Since the defendants 
have already contested the matter and their interest has been 
adequately represented in the proceeding no separate 
adjudication is necessary for the purpose of the present Rule. 
Accordingly the said application is disposed of on the 
observation that the judgment passed in this Rule shall equally 
bind the applicants as they claim under the defendants. 
The order of stay passed by this Court stands vacated.  
 
Communicate this judgment to the concerned Court and 
send down the lower Courts’ record.  
 
 
Md. Ali Reza, J:

explanation: Applying Sections 42, 43, and 72 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950 alongside Section 114(e) of the Evidence Act, the Court held the October 1978 Gazette declaring final publication of the Compensation Assessment Roll—naming plaintiffs' predecessors and imparting constructive notice—conclusively vested the cattle-market property in the Government free from encumbrances and barred a 2002 title suit. <<PAGE 1>>
In the Supreme Court of Bangladesh 
High Court Division 
(Civil Revisional Jurisdiction) 
Present: 
Mr. Justice Md. Riaz Uddin Khan 
 
Civil Revision No. 5276 of 2023  
  
IN THE MATTER OF : 
An application under section 115(4) of the Code of 
Civil Procedure 
-And- 
In the Matter of: 
A.B.M. Anwarul Islam 
        ... Defendant-Petitioner 
 
 
Versus 
Dilip Kumar Nath and others 
... Plaintiff-Opposite parties 
Mr. Maqbul Ahmed, with 
Mr. Md. Saiful Quader Chowdhury, Advocates 
                                .... For the petitioner 
 
 
 
No one 
                                                                                          … For the opposite party 
Judgment on: 09.03.2026 
 
Md. Riaz Uddin Khan, J: 
 
 
At the instance of the defendant Rule was issued 
asking the opposite parties to show cause as to why the 
judgment and order dated 27.02.2023 passed by the 
leaned District Judge, Chattogram in Civil Revision No. 
12 of 2023 allowing the Civil Revision and reversing 
the judgment and order dated 24.11.2022 passed by the 
learned Senior Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, Chattogram 
in Other Suit No. 266 of 2011 should not be set aside 
and or such other or further order or orders should not 
be passed as to this Court may deem fit and 
appropriate. 
At the time of issuance of the Rule all further 
proceedings of Other Suit No. 266 of 2011 pending in 
the court of Senior Assistant Judge, 3rd Court, 

<<PAGE 2>>
 
2
Chattogram was stayed initially for a period of 
03(three) months which was extended time to time. 
Short fact for disposal of this Rule is that 
opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff filed other suit No. 
142 of 1998 (re numbered as other suit No. 266 of 2011) 
against the defendants including the present petitioner 
for declaration of title, recovery of khas possession 
and for permanent injunction. The defendant petitioner 
contested the suit by filing written statement denying 
all the material facts as alleged in the plaint. 
However, at one stage of the suit when it was for 
peremptory hearing the plaintiff filed an application 
for directing the defendant No. 1 to submit the power 
of attorney being deed No. 1418 dated 08.09.1998 and 
also to produce the executants of the power of attorney 
before the court along with their National Identity 
Cards. After hearing the parties the application was 
rejected by the trial court by order No. 204 dated 
24.11.2022. Against that order the plaintiff filed 
Civil Revision No. 12 of 2023 before the District 
Judge, Chattogram. The learned District Judge fixed the 
matter 
for 
hearing 
of 
the 
maintainability/ 
admissibility and by order No. 2 dated 27.02.2023 the 
learned District Judge without admitting the same by 
the impugned judgment and order dated 27.02.2023 
allowed the revision in part directing the defendant 
No.1 to produce the executants of the power of attorney 
before the trial court.          
Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said 
judgment and order dated 27.02.2023 passed by the 
District Judge, Chattogram the defendant No.1 as 
petitioner filed the instant civil revision before this 

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
court and obtained the rule and order of stay as stated 
at the very outset. 
Mr. Maqbul Ahmed along with Mr. Md. Saiful Quader 
Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing for the 
defendant-petitioner submits that the trial court 
giving reason rightly rejected the application while 
the learned District Judge without admitting the 
revision allowed the same without assigning any reason 
which is liable to be set aside.  
Mr. Ahemd then submits that according to the 
plaintiff the executants reside in India and in that 
view of the fact the learned District Judge has 
exceeded his jurisdiction allowing such application 
while Rule 4 of Order-V of the Code of Civil Procedure 
clearly imposed embargo upon the court not to direct 
any party to appear in person before it unless he 
resides within the local limits of the court’s ordinary 
jurisdiction subject to some conditions. 
Mr. Ahmed lastly submits that the petitioner being 
the defendant is to prove his case by adducing and 
producing witness and documents at the trial but while      
he did not submit any power of attorney before the 
court, the plaintiff cannot pray to produce such 
documents along with the executants who according to 
the plaintiff resides out of Bangladesh.  
No one appears to oppose this Rule.  
I have heard the learned advocate for the 
petitioner, perused the application. I have also gone 
through the orders passed by the court below. 
According to the learned advocate the court cannot 
pass any order directing the executants of the power of 
attorney to be present in person before the court who 

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
are 
according 
to 
the 
plaintiff 
resides 
outside 
Bangladesh. Let us now see the provision of Order-5, 
Rule-3 and 4 which reads as follows- 
Order-V, Rule 3- (1) Where the Court sees reason 
to require the personal appearance of the defendant, 
the summons shall order him to appear in person in 
Court on the day therein specified.  
(2) Where the Court sees reason to require the 
personal appearance of the plaintiff on the same day, 
it shall make an order for such appearance.  
Rule 4 – No party shall be ordered to appear in 
person unless he resides- 
(a) within the local  limits of the Court’s 
ordinary original jurisdiction or 
(b) without such limits but at a place less than 
fifty or (where there is railway or steamer 
communication or other established public 
conveyance for five-sixths of the distance 
between the place where he resides and the 
place where the Court is situate) less than 
two hundred miles distance from the court-
house.    
It appears from the above provisions of law that 
some limitations have been imposed upon the Court in 
regard to ordering the parties to be present in person 
but in the instant case admittedly the persons directed 
to be present before the Court is neither the plaintiff 
nor the defendants. For proper adjudication, the Code 
of Civil Procedure has given ample authority to the 
Court asking anyone to be present in person before the 
court or asking anyone to produce any documents which 
is producible as evidence. Section 30 of the Code of 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
Civil Procedure is the provision under which the Court 
can exercise such jurisdiction which reads as follows-  
“30. Subject to such conditions and limitations as 
may be prescribed the Court may, at any time, either of 
its own motion or on the application of any party,-  
(a) make such orders as  may be necessary or 
reasonable in all matters relating to the 
delivery and answering of interrogatories, 
the admission of documents and facts, and 
the discovery, inspection, production, 
impounding and return of documents or 
other 
material 
objects 
producible 
as 
evidence;  
(b) issue 
summonses 
to 
persons 
whose 
attendance is required either to give 
evidence or to produce documents or such 
other objects as aforesaid.  
(c) order any fact to be proved by affidavit.   
From plain reading of Section 30 as above it is 
apparent and obvious that subject to such conditions 
and limitations as may be prescribed, the Court may at 
any time either of its own motion or on the application 
of the party make such order as may be necessary or 
reasonable in all matters relating to the delivery and 
answering 
of 
interrogatories, 
the 
admission 
of 
documents and facts and the discovery inspection, 
production, impounding and return of documents or other 
material object producible as evidence can issue 
summons to persons whose attendance is required either 
to give evidence or to produce documents or such other 
objects as aforesaid and order any fact to be proved by 
affidavit. It is the Court’s discretion in the given 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
facts to decide whether any one’s presence in Court is 
required 
or 
not. 
This 
discretion 
is 
judicial 
discretion, not whimsical. So, the contention of the 
learned advocate, that Court cannot ask anyone to 
appear in person before it who resides outside the 
ordinary jurisdiction of the Court or beyond the two 
hundred miles from the Court-house, has no legs to 
stand. 
Be that as it may, let me now examine whether in 
the present case the learned District Judge has rightly 
passed the order directing the executants of the power 
of attorney to be present before the trial court. In 
the application filed by the plaintiff for directing 
the defendant No. 1 to produce the power of attorney 
and the executants of the power of attorney along with 
their National Identity Cards, it appears that the 
plaintiff claimed some contradictory allegations: in 
the one hand he claimed that the executants of the 
power of attorney do not reside in Bangladesh rather 
they reside in India, on the other hand he claims that 
two of the three executants are dead. It is further 
claimed that at the time of so-called execution of the 
power of Attorney which is a forged one, the executants 
were not in Bangladesh and by false personation it was 
registered. The defendant claims the property on the 
strength of the power of attorney but yet to produce 
the same before the trial court.  
As per sections 101 to 103 of the Evidence Act, 
the onus of proof of any fact lies upon the party who 
claim that fact. In the present case to proving the 
defendants case if the defendants produce or rely on 
any document such as the said Power of Attorney, then 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
the Court can examine that power of Attorney as to 
whether it is genuine or not and the plaintiff will get 
his opportunity to proof that the same is forged by 
adducing evidence and further to prove that at the time 
of execution the executants were not in Bangladesh or 
the same was created by false personation. The learned 
judge of the trial court has given the reasons for not 
accepting the application and according to Section 30 
of the Code of Civil Procedure it is the trial court 
who has the discretion to allow such application or 
not. Even the Court at his own motion can ask any 
person to be present or to produce any document 
producible in evidence. The trial court thought it 
proper at this stage of the suit not to allow such 
application while the learned District Judge without 
assigning any reason at the time of hearing the 
admissibility of the revision allowed such revision 
directing the executants to be present in person before 
the trial court by his impugned judgment and order 
which is not only illogical but also without any basis. 
In the given facts at the stage of the case the order 
directing the defendants to produce the executants 
before the trial court in person has no reason to be 
sustained. In such view of the matter, I have no option 
but to interfere with the order passed by the learned 
District Judge, Chattogram.    
In the result the Rule is made absolute and the 
judgment and order dated 27.02.2023 passed by the 
learned District Judge, Chattogram in Civil Revision 
no.12 of 2023 is hereby set aside and the order dated 
24.11.2022 passed by the trial court is affirmed. 

<<PAGE 8>>
 
8
It 
is 
very 
unfortunate 
that 
the 
defendant 
petitioner obtained an order of stay of all further 
proceedings of the suit instead of stay operation of 
the impugned order. As such the trial of the suit could 
not be held for more than two years. However, the order 
of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated. 
The trial court is directed to proceed with the 
case expeditiously keeping in mind that the original 
suit was filed in the year 1998. 
Communicate the judgment and order at once.  
    
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Ziaul Karim 
Bench Officer
input_summary: First OPPOSITE PARTY brought a 1998 civil suit (renumbered in 2011) against first-defendant PETITIONER and co-defendants seeking declaratory title, recovery of khas possession, and permanent injunction, which PETITIONER contested by written statement. At the peremptory hearing stage, the plaintiff applied to compel PETITIONER to file a power of attorney dated 08.09.1998 and produce its executants in person with their National Identity Cards. After the trial court turned down that plea on 24.11.2022, the plaintiff filed a civil revision before the District Judge, who on 27.02.2023—at the admissibility hearing without admitting the revision—ordered PETITIONER to produce the executants in court. Moving unopposed under Section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure, PETITIONER invoked Order V Rule 4 regarding foreign residents and noted he had not yet tendered the instrument.
explanation: Distinguishing Order V Rules 3 and 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908—which restrict personal-appearance orders only as to parties—the Court held Section 30 vests judicial discretion in the trial court to summon witnesses or documents. Given the plaintiff's contradictory claims that the executants lived abroad while two of three were dead, and since PETITIONER bore the burden under Sections 101-103 of the Evidence Act if he ever tendered the power of attorney, the District Judge acted without basis in reversing the trial court's reasoned refusal without admitting the revision.

In the instant revision Rule was issued on 12.06.2024 
calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the 
impugned judgment and decree dated 26.05.2024 passed by 
the learned Joint District Judge, 2nd Court, Dinajpur in Other

learned Assistant Judge, Kaharol, Dinajpur in Other Class Suit 
No. 56 of 2015 (308 of 2009) dismissing the suit should not be 
set aside and/or such other of further order or orders passed as

The predecessor of the opposite parties as plaintiff 
instituted Other Class Suit No. 308 of 2009 on 01.12.2009 in 
the Court of the Senior Assistant Judge, Dinajpur which was 
subsequently renumbered as Other Suit No. 56 of 2015 
praying for a declaration that the judgment and decree dated 
18.09.2005 passed in Other Suit No. 40 of 1996 as described 
in schedule ‘Kha’ to the plaint in respect of the suit house 
described in schedule ‘Ka’ are false, collusive, inoperative, 
without lawful basis, fraudulent, illegal and not binding upon 
the plaintiff. By amendment dated 17.09.2017 plaintiff also 
prayed for declaration against the deed dated 19.02.2007.  

<<PAGE 3>>
 
3
The facts, in brief, are that the non-bangali plaintiff 
sometime in the year 1961-1962 applied to the Office of the 
Administrative Officer, Dinajpur Sub-Town Housing Estate 
for allotment of House Number U/1 situated in Block No. 5 of 
the said Housing Estate at Dinajpur Sub-Town for permanent 
residence of himself and his family. Upon approval of the said 
application by defendant 4 in his capacity as Chairman of the 
Allotment Committee under the order of defendant 3 the 
Housing Estate authority issued an allotment letter to the 
plaintiff by memorandum dated 12.08.1966 for allotment of 
the house described in schedule ‘Ka’ to the plaint. At that time 
an amount of Tk. 180 was received from the plaintiff and he 
was directed to execute an agreement with the Government in

<<PAGE 4>>
 
4
Thereafter on behalf of the then Government of East 
Pakistan the Administrative Officer, Housing Estate, Dinajpur 
and the plaintiff executed an agreement in respect of the said 
house for a term of 99 years which was registered in the Sadar 
Sub-Registry Office, Dinajpur as Agreement Deed No. 17421 
on 14.11.1966 and 05.12.1966 respectively. Subsequently in 
accordance with the Government circular dated 12.01.1964 
possession of the said house was delivered to the plaintiff on 
24.11.1966. Thereafter the plaintiff started residing in the suit 
house with his family while regularly paying the government 
dues and taxes. Subsequently the plaintiff left the said house 
under the care of his sister and went to Dhaka in connection 
with his service. During that period the plaintiff’s sister 
allowed defendant 1 to reside in one room of the suit house 
without rent. Taking advantage of the simplicity of the 

<<PAGE 5>>
 
5
plaintiff’s sister and the temporary absence of the plaintiff the 
said defendant 1 namely Shafiqul Alam in collusion with some 
dishonest employees of the Housing Estate authority managed 
to procure an offer letter in respect of the said house on 
05.02.1992 without the knowledge of the plaintiff and paid the 
first installment of the price. However he failed to execute and 
register the lease deed in accordance with clause 6 of the 
allotment conditions. Thereafter when the plaintiff returned to 
Dinajpur from his workplace at Dhaka and came to the said 
quarter he came to learn through local sources and by making 
inquiry in the Housing Office that defendant 1 had 
fraudulently and illegally obtained allotment of the house by 
way of collusion and deception. Consequently on 05.03.1994 
the plaintiff filed an application before defendant 4 seeking 
restoration of the said house in his favour. Upon such 

<<PAGE 6>>
 
6
application defendant 4 by order dated 04.05.1994 directed 
cancellation of the offer letter issued in the name of defendant 
No. 1 and forwarded the matter to defendant 2 for approval. 
Thereafter by memorandum dated 14.11.1995 defendant 2 
directed that the possession of the suit house be handed over to 
the plaintiff within 15 days after issuing notice to defendant 1. 
Accordingly notice was issued to defendant 1. Thereafter the 
plaintiff having been informed that he would receive further 
communication from the office at the address mentioned in his 
application returned to his workplace at Dhaka. It is further 
stated that at the time of cancellation of the plaintiff’s lease the 
Housing Estate authority, Dinajpur did not serve any notice 
upon the plaintiff. After a long lapse of time as the plaintiff 
did not receive any communication or information regarding 
the suit house he became anxious and on 19.10.2009 went to 

<<PAGE 7>>
 
7
the office of defendant 2 at Dinajpur Sub-Town and inquired 
about delivery of possession of the suit house. At that time 
defendant 2 informed the plaintiff for the first time that 
defendant 1 had filed Other Suit 40 of 1996 in the Court of the 
Senior Assistant Judge and obtained an exparte decree therein.  
Being astonished the plaintiff collected an information 
slip on 22.10.2009 and thereby came to know for the first time 
about the exparte proceedings of the said suit. Thereafter he 
inspected the record of the said case on 08.11.2009 and 
subsequently obtained certified copies of the judgment and 
decree as well as the written statements of defendants 2 and 4 
on 19.11.2009 whereupon the entire matter became clear to 
the plaintiff.   
It appears from the written statements of defendants 2 
and 4 that upon the application of the plaintiff the allotment 

<<PAGE 8>>
 
8
issued in the name of defendant 1 had already been cancelled. 
The defendant 1 however by practising fraud upon the Court 
in Other Suit 40 of 1996 obtained the impugned judgment and 
decree by suppressing material facts and by not impleading the 
plaintiff as a necessary party to the said suit although the 
plaintiff was a necessary and proper party thereto. Had the 
plaintiff been impleaded as a party in that suit defendant 1 
could never have obtained the impugned judgment and decree. 
It is further stated that the father of defendant 1 by practising 
fraud and deception prepared a false power of attorney in the 
name of his son who was residing abroad and conducted the 
said suit on the basis of such forged authority thereby 
obtaining an exparte judgment and decree in a wholly illegal 
manner which is not binding upon the plaintiff. Since the said 
judgment and decree if allowed to stand would cause

9
irreparable loss and injury to the plaintiff the plaintiff was 
constrained to institute the present suit.  
The petitioner as defendant 1 entered appearance and 
contested the suit by filing a written statement denying all the 
material allegations made in the plaint contending inter alia 
that the suit in its present form and manner is not maintainable 
in law and the statements made in the plaint are false, 
fabricated and concocted and the suit is barred by the 
principles of estoppel, waiver and acquiescence. The case of 
defendant 1 in substance is that although the plaintiff had 
taken lease of the house described in schedule ‘Ka’ to the 
plaint from defendant 2 in the year 1964 the said lease was 
cancelled in the year 1986 due to the plaintiff’s failure to pay 
the entire installments of the lease money. Though an order for 
lease of the house described in schedule ‘Ka’ was once passed

10
in favour of the plaintiff he never obtained possession of the 
said house rather the suit house remained in the possession 
and enjoyment of the plaintiff’s sister namely Sokina Khatun. 
After cancellation of the allotment in the name of the plaintiff 
the plaintiff’s sister had no lawful authority to continue 
residing in the said house and she also lacked the financial 
capacity to obtain a fresh lease upon payment of the required 
consideration. Consequently when she intended to relinquish 
possession of the said house she transferred possession thereof 
in the year 1991 in favour of defendant 1 without any 
registered deed.  
Thereafter defendant 1 submitted a written application to 
defendant 2 the Administrative Officer for allotment of the 
said house. Pursuant to the said application defendants 2-4 
allotted the said house to defendant 1. After obtaining the 

<<PAGE 11>>
 
11
allotment defendant 1 took possession of the suit house and 
started paying municipal taxes to the Dinajpur Municipality in 
due course. He also deposited the first installment amounting 
to Tk. 6,882 on 16.06.1992 through treasury challan and 
purchased eight non-judicial stamps valued at Tk. 5,555 for 
the purpose of execution and registration of the lease deed of 
the said house. Defendant 1 also made repeated requests to 
defendants 2-4 for registration of the lease deed in his favour. 
However in the meantime defendant 1 decided to go to Oman 
in the Middle East for employment. Prior to leaving the 
country in the middle of November 1992 he executed a power 
of attorney appointing his father Shamsul Alam as his attorney 
to take necessary steps for registration of the kabala deed in 
respect of the suit house in his favour. While pursuing the 
matter before the offices of defendants 2-4 for registration of 

<<PAGE 12>>
 
12
the deed in favour of defendant 1 the said attorney came to 
learn that the file relating to the suit house had been forwarded 
to the office of defendant 3 at Dhaka and without the said file 
it would not be possible to register the deed. Thereafter the 
father of defendant 1 came to know for the first time on 
27.04.1996 from the office of defendant 2 through Memo 
Number 265 dated 23.04.1996 that the allotment granted in 
favour of defendant 1 had been cancelled. However prior to 
cancellation of the said allotment no show cause notice had 
been served upon defendant 1 and the allotment was cancelled 
without his knowledge. Accordingly defendant 1 instituted 
Other Suit 40 of 1996 seeking a declaration that the order
